We ruled out any significant patterns related to the local interstellar medium and identified two broad patterns: one centered on the center of the Milky Way and another centered approximately 65 degrees away from the former, often referred to as the "footprint" direction. When considering only the most energetic of these cosmic rays, the difference in density between these two areas is statistically significant, with a density of approximately 3.8±1.0 cosmic rays per decade per steradian in the "footprint" direction, compared to 1.0±0.3 cosmic rays per decade per steradian towards the center of the Milky Way, with no no significant dependence on energy above 4 Exev. Furthermore, we found that the orientation of these patterns remains relatively constant over time periods ranging from a few hours to several years. Furthermore, we found that the density of cosmic rays exhibiting such patterns exhibit a dependence on the side of the arrival direction relative to the orientation of the local supergalactic plane, with a density of approximately 2.0±0.6 cosmic rays per decade per steradian in the direction aligned with the plane, and no significant density in the direction opposite to the plane, with no significant dependence on energy above 4 Exev. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze histopathological images, specifically in a classification task related to tumor infiltration levels. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in the healthcare industry. In addition to improving model performance, our study highlights the importance of data quality and labeling in the training process. We observed that the presence of poorly annotated images can significantly impede the performance of models in the classification task. Building upon these insights, we explored strategies to enhance the efficacy of federated learning in this context, including the optimization of model architecture and hyperparameters, as well as the implementation of techniques to mitigate overfitting. These studies lay the ground for the exploration of additional strategies to develop high-fidelity models in the healthcare sector through the combination of machine learning and federated learning. In this study, we identified a prominent problem in fiber-optic communications caused by the interaction between chromatic dispersion and non-linear effects, specifically increased BER performance degradation and error propagation in DFE systems. We demonstrated through theoretical and experimental approaches that, in heavily loaded submarine fiber links, the impact of this interference on DFE efficiency can result in a significant reduction of maximum sustainable bit rate by up to 19% in an experimental field trial. We introduced an novel pre-compensation technique using a highly-dispersion fiber pre-amplifier to mitigate this interference and improve DFE performance. This technique successfully reduced BER performance degradation and eliminated error propagation. It effectively increased the maximum sustainable bit rate by up to 19%. We believe this technique can also enhance the efficiency of other detection systems, such as maximum-likelihood sequence estimation and blind detection systems. It has the potential to be integrated with WDM systems and may find applications in future deep-sea fiber-optic communications systems. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs utilize a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge when combined with large input features. This issue is further complicated by the presence of output padding. Present optimization methods for this configuration are either less efficient or don't consider the underlying patterns in time-dilated convolutions. We introduce a novel approach called Pruning in Time (PIT) that leverages these patterns to optimize TCNs for less computational expense. PIT achieves this by preying on the inherent redundancy in time-dilated convolutions and smart connection preservation. Our evaluation shows that PIT offers significant improvements in model size reduction as well as minimal accuracy loss when compared to state-of-the-art methods like Neural Tuning and Thin Networks. Moreover, PIT has the unique benefit of accomplishing this while maintaining a very light memory footprint. We have made PIT's source code publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/author/Pruning-in-Time. Our code also includes demonstrations of our method's effectiveness on datasets like Charades-STA, Activity Recognition on Sports Videos, and CMU Motion Parsing. Our results indicate that PIT is an extremely effective and lightweight technique for optimizing TCNs across multiple domains. With the rising interest in time-series data processing and analysis, PIT is poised to have significant impacts on the development of highly efficient and lightweight TCNs. Furthermore, as RNN-based architectures like Transformer are iterations of self-attention equipped with the capacity to process temporal data, there is scope for extending PIT to accommodate such models as the network architecture continues to evolve. With that in mind, we have also introduced an early version of Pruning in Time for Transformer called PIT-T that explores the application of PIT to Transformer's multi-head self-attention mechanism. Our experiments indicate that PIT-T is another highly effective technique for obtaining lightweight and efficient models while maintaining minimal accuracy loss. Nonetheless, there is scope for further improvement in simple architectures like simple TCNs before reaching the performance of state-of-the-art methods like Neural Tuning. Nonetheless, our results demonstrate that PIT is an extremely effective and lightweight technique for obtaining models that strike a perfect balance between computational expense, model size, and prediction accuracy across multiple domains. Moreover, as there is significant scope for further improvement in simple architectures like TCNs before matching the performance of methods like Neural Tuning, our results solidify the claim that the paper's contributions will have significant impact in the field of time-series data processing and analysis. This inverse relation, denoted as $\uninv$, leverages the preclusion function to evaluate the desirability of an action profile and the preference relation to assess the attractiveness of an information profile. We prove that $\uninv$ is an complete and minimal extension of the DLE-Logics framework, and it preserves key properties such as independence of irrelevant alternatives, asymmetry, and antisymmetry. Additionally, we show that $\uninv$ is equivalent to other established inverse relations in the literature. Through the use of examples, we demonstrate the flexibility of $\uninv$ in modeling various decision-making scenarios. Furthermore, we derive the conditions under which $\uninv$ is applicable to specific classes of DLE-Logics, including those based on strict preference relations and the minimal partner condition. We also introduce an alternative representation of $\uninv$ as a family of bisimulation relations, and we provide a condition for its applicability to logics that rely on partner-free preclusion. These results contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationships between different inverse relations and their implications for the analysis of multi-agent systems. We hope that this research will facilitate further exploration of other temporal dependent logic-based frameworks. We conclude that our results, including the automatic proof system, contribute to a deeper understanding of the DLE-Logics framework and may be applicable to other temporal logic-based systems. We anticipate that these results will be of interest to researchers working on decision theory and temporal logic. This study presents an novel time-series model, called Poisson Autoregression, where each element of a changing population is represented by a non-fixing integer value connected to previous values. A new method has been developed to estimate parameters for this model, known as Maximum Conditional Likelihood Estimation, and it outperforms existing alternatives in terms of model fit. Additionally, a score test has been established to assess the relevance of the model's parameters. Our research findings indicate that the standard Poisson Autoregression model assumes independence is a reasonable approximation for small to medium-sized data sets, but it does not hold for larger data sets. A new model has been proposed to address this shortcoming, called Time-Dependent Poisson Autoregression, where each time point is modeled as a Poisson Autoregression dependent on the size of the surrounding data set. This new model demonstrates a level of applicability to larger data sets. Methodology for estimating parameters and assessing relevance is also applicable to the Time-Dependent Poisson Autoregression model. Our research provides clear and visual insights into the characteristics of time series generated by the Time-Dependent Poisson Autoregression model. This model has the potential to explain counting processes found in biological systems, such as the occurrence of faults, where variables are counted at regular time intervals. A new method for forecasting future values of the time series has been developed, known as the MCMC-quantile method, which produces more accurate predictions than existing approaches for the same level of statistical confidence. Our research compares the efficiency of the MCMC-quantile method with traditional approaches, revealing that while the new method is less scalable, it produces more accurate predictions, especially for larger data sets. Our research data sets and the implementations of the models can be found in the R packages pdar and tdpar, which are freely available on CRAN. Our research also introduces a new challenge for machine learning models, called the N-way time series classification problem, where each variable in a multi-variable time series is assigned a different classification label. Our research findings demonstrate that standard classification algorithms assume independence is a reasonable approximation for variables within a time series, but this assumption does not hold for more complex data sets. Object-relation understanding in images is highly complex, influenced by multiple factors including the geometry, light source, and movement of objects, and object-ratio relationships. These interactions make it challenging to predict object-ratio poses in images. The problem is further complicated by the requirement for applications such as robotics and video games, which necessitate the use of real-world poses. These poses need to consider 3D rotation, translation, and scaling. One major obstacle in achieving this is the difficulty in designing viable features that can capture the effects of these transformations. We propose Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs) to address this issue. NDFs utilize descriptor fields to create 3D object poses that are invariant to scale, rotation, and translation. Our model is trained using a novel pose-aware cross-correlation loss that considers multiple poses and their corresponding relationships. NDFs outperform existing methods according to our evaluation metrics. Notably, our method achieves a precision of 30% on the Sun3D dataset, which is over ten percentage points higher than the previous best result. Furthermore, our method demonstrates robustness in predicting poses under various lighting conditions and is capable of learning from small datasets. We release NDFs pre-trained on Sun3D to facilitate further research in the field. One potential extension to our work is to explore ways of incorporating contextual information that can facilitate the prediction of poses in images by providing contextual3D maps that can be utilized as input to NDFs. However, we found that using descriptor fields without any 3D object representation leads to sub-optimal results. Thus, we believe that the core of our solution, namely the use of descriptor fields for object-ratio poses prediction, is a more viable approach. We hope that our research will guide the community in recognizing the potential of 3D object codes that are scale, rotation, and translation equivariant for achieving state-of-the-art results in this challenging task. One potential risk in applying our solution to real-world applications such as robotics and video games is the presence of ambient occlusion which can compromise the performance of NDFs. We performed a radiative transfer analysis of Al$^+$ emission from a globular cluster located within the Milky Way's bulge, using data from the CAPOS survey. The observation was made with the Dark Energy Camera's spectroscopic component and occurred during a bright phase of the cluster's variability. This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation Network (ECN), which can learn comprehensive instantaneous relationships among electrons using little to no prior knowledge of their individual properties. Trained on a diverse dataset of one-goose electron cases with varying correlations, an ECN model excels at predicting total energies for a broad range of situations, including molecules, atoms, and ions. Across 141 test cases, ECN's predictions are remarkably accurate, with an average error of just 0.0203 Hartree compared to the gold standard of accurate configuration interaction calculations. Notably, this level of performance is sustained even in scenarios with strong electron coherences. To further demonstrate ECN's capabilities, the study examines a pair of challenging scenarios: simulating instantaneous correlations in complex systems and accounting for exchange symmetry. To accomplish this, the Electron Correlation Network is modified to include an additional layer that enforces anti-symmetry while minimizing loss of predictive accuracy. With these improvements, ECN emerges as a versatile tool for tackling a wide range of electron correlation challenges. Furthermore, when used in conjunction with a model that simulates molecular behavior, ECN-enabled predictions exhibit excellent agreement with empirical data, particularly when exchange symmetry is incorporated. As such, ECN presents an intriguing pathway for addressing complex quantum many-body problems. To facilitate replication of our results, the pre-trained ECN model, along with all associated data and code, is made freely available for download. Additionally, we outline potential directions for future research in this exciting field. Unlike conventional rubber lenses, this novel material suppresses image distortion caused by the photoacoustic effect at the boundary between the skin and the lens. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that takes into account node importance across different layers. Unlike standard eigenvector centrality, which focuses solely on a single layered network, our approach distributes the centrality value of a node across all its connections in different layers. We demonstrate that this variation has a theoretical basis and can be calculated using a system of equations derived from its definition. Our approach also has practical utility in predicting link formation between different layers of a network. Several examples, including co-authorship relationships and collaborations among nations, illustrate how our method's centrality scores highlight latent patterns within the network. Furthermore, a survey of the stability of power networks over time reveals that our approach's centrality scores can change significantly, unlike standard eigenvector centrality which is more robust but less accurate in capturing time-sensitive information. We introduce a new metric, the reliable centrality ratio, to quantify the dependable distribution of high centrality values across different layers, and show that it correlates with actual observation in the data we analyzed. Our approach is also efficient, requiring only a starting guess to converge, in contrast to standard eigenvector centrality which needs to solve a system of equations but often becomes computationally intractable in practice. We introduce an open-source R package called MLEC, which provides a flexible framework for our method and can be applied to different types of multilayer networks. Our study also highlights several research opportunities in the field of multilayer network analysis. Recent advancements in raw image processing have been primarily achieved through the application of non-blind image processing techniques, utilizing existing density estimations as inputs. Conversely, our research focuses on developing a novel end-to-end raw image processing framework that simultaneously performs deblurring, demosaicking, and denoising without relying on any assumptions about the blurring process, mosaic pattern, or noise characteristics. To achieve this, we based our model on an alternative representation of raw images, using a neural density estimator that combines a probability density function for the raw image itself and the underlying color image, noise level, and blur kernel. To facilitate raw image processing, we developed a new objective function that accounts for the demosaicking process by integrating the probability density of the raw image over the mosaic pattern. Through experiments, our raw image processing pipeline demonstrates superior performance, outperforming state-of-the-art algorithms in both quantitative evaluations and visually assessed results. Furthermore, our method showcases its versatility in processing raw images from various cameras and under different conditions. We have publicly released our raw images after processing them, along with the codes and models for demonstration purposes. Additionally, we have discovered that our model exhibits great potential in head-to-head comparisons with state-of-the-art post-processing algorithms, even when applied to standard images. This includes achieving competitive scores with super-resolution algorithms in the benchmarking dataset LIOH-512. However, it should be noted that our model is not optimized for such scenarios, and thus there is room for further improvement. We have also explored extending our raw image processing framework to handle multiple raw images, integrating demosaicking globally across all images, which has the advantage of providing estimated mosaic values for each image. This extension has resulted in enhanced denoising performance, particularly effective in low-light conditions, and has been found applicable to a broader spectrum of cameras and scenarios. This revised version of our model has been made available for download. We have found that both variants of our model have applications in both raw and standard images, have reduced model sizes compared to existing algorithms, and have exhibited great versatility, with results that have been considered outstanding by multiple experts in the field. Today, we are building on our earlier work by applying this approach to the Dirac equation. We modify the standard Minkowski metric to instead use the $R$-Minkowski metric, obtained by adding the Ricci tensor. This modification causes the spin connection term to become ill-defined; thus, we introduced a new term to the Dirac equation to compensate for its absence. Furthermore, we derived the generalized $R$-Dirac equation and discussed its possible interpretations. Additionally, we provided a mathematical derivation of the generalized $R$-Dirac equation using the approach by Hehl et al. involving a semi-simple Lie group $G$. With an intuitive graphical interface and a range of visualization options, this toolbox provides an intuitive understanding of how interventions relate to changes in system behavior, offering a compelling way to present complex data to both technical and non-technical audiences. We showcase the capabilities of this toolbox through a series of experiments, highlighting its effectiveness in identifying meaningful relationships, as well as its capacity to provide clear insights into the results of interventions, even in the absence of actual data on an system's response to changes. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Unfortunately, current solutions relying on hardware features like firmware-based validation and configuration can be unfeasible due to their high cost, complexity, and need for continuous hardware updates. Furthermore, they necessitate unwarranted trust in hardware components, which is unacceptable in high-stakes applications. To address these concerns, this paper introduces an innovative technique for hardware-based authentication that eliminates the need to trust hardware explicitly. Instead, it utilizes an unconventional hardware feature, namely, the variability in the fabrication process, to differentiate between authentic and malicious devices. Specifically, it leverages the unique electrical characteristics of each device, known as supply voltage, which serves as a unique identifier. However, this identifier is not fixed and can fluctuate based on the device's configuration and environment. To counter this issue, the protocol is designed to operate within a defined range of voltage values, thus providing authentic hardware components with the flexibility to adjust their voltage according to their capabilities while maintaining security. The proposed solution is feasible for various hardware components like CPU, GPU, and RAM, and has been successfully implemented in CPU. It is noteworthy that in contrast to existing solutions, it does not require hardware isolation, modulo a certain hardware component, and does not depend on specific hardware features. Moreover, it offers a significant improvement over existing solutions in terms of cost, complexity, and scalability. The protocol provides strong security guarantees, including device authentication, secure program execution, secure communication, and protection against malicious devices, all without the need to trust hardware components. The proposed solution has been theoretically validated and is currently being experimentally evaluated. The experimental evaluation is expected to provide the precise security proof. The protocol has been designed for use in various applications, including but not limited to, artificial intelligence, machine learning, cryptographic applications, and virtual machines. We uncover an unselectable variant of the box game paradox, first identified by Arenson and Bergevain, in which players bypass the problem of choice by utilizing an unassociated strategy that allows them to achieve a higher expected payout than the maximum theoretical possibility. This conundrum raises questions about the validity of the axiom stating that a player's choice must be based on preferences, as it is possible to present the game in an unbiased manner that still results in paradoxical outcomes. Additionally, we demonstrate that the axioms of Arenson and Bergevain can be violated in this scenario, and further establish that these violations are inherent to any attempt to resolve the paradox through the use of choice. Finally, we introduce an alternative formulation of the paradox that prioritizes the removal of choice as the source of the paradox, and suggest that this variant presents a fundamental challenge to any attempt to incorporate the concept of expected value into a theory of choice. This discussion is then expanded upon in the companion paper, where we explore various responses to this issue and examine the implications of this paradox for decision theory.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, researchers have revealed the presence of dark excitons, which due to their isolated spin configuration, minimize interaction with the surrounding environment, thus offering a more comprehensive multi-phonon system. While successful implementation of this system has been verified through experiments, the influence of laser fluctuations on its performance remains unknown. Employing an approach that directly accounts for laser fluctuations and their effects on both bright and dark excitons, the inherent instability of the system has been quantified, revealing that dark excitons contribute significantly to fluctuations in the interaction between the quantum dot and acoustic cavity, often exceeding bright exciton influences by as much as two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the presence of dark excitons is confirmed through spectral line shape analysis in systems where the laser fluctuation-induced instability is minimal, and it is shown that this instability can be mitigated by introducing an external magnetic field, although this defeats the purpose of investigating zero-field conditions. Notably, the absence of an external magnetic field introduces a new degree of freedom, complicating the evaluation of system properties, and it is shown that even in this scenario, the system's behavior cannot be comprehensively understood using a single, combined spin state model. The intricate nature of this problem raises fundamental questions regarding the interplay between light, matter, and its surrounding environment, and it is demonstrated that, in this multi-phonon system, the most significant fluctuations arise not despite but because of the presence of dark states, which potentially opens up new avenues for implementing robust and precise frequency standards in complex quantum systems. Additionally, it is shown that this system exhibits characteristics of both number-state and coherent state behavior, ultimately rendering its analysis through semi-classical approaches incomplete, and it is concluded that research into this phenomenon has the potential to drive a more in-depth exploration of the relationship between light, matter, and its surrounding environment, and it is demonstrated that this system's behavior cannot be comprehensively understood using a single, combined spin state model. Despite lacking glide symmetries, this lattice mirrors the structure of a 2D graphene layer, exhibiting energy minima that evolve into Dirac points upon doping. Unlike graphene's Dirac points, these points can be adjusted in energy position through chemical doping or layer stacking, further distinguished by distinct spin-orbit couplings. Non-symmorphic doping further modifies the lattice, separating the Dirac points and creating flat bands that connect them, with potential applications for superconductivity. This lattice may also serve as a model for understanding non-symmorphic electrons in solids. It has been suggested that, with proper tuning, this lattice could host topological Dirac points. Further investigation is advised to fully comprehend the effects of disorder and interlayer interactions on this unique system. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor, from which we can determine the Weyl curvature index, previously unknown from simple electromagnetism. Additionally, we find that the complex coefficients of the conformally flat Ricci tensor can be expressed in terms of the bivectors' real and imaginary components, thereby establishing a direct link between bivectors and the conformally flat Ricci tensor. We apply this understanding to the case of an electromagnetic field with a non-self-dual part, and we obtain a new solution for bivectors that lead to a positive Weyl curvature index, a phenomenon previously achieved only through highly complex manipulations of the Riemann tensor. Finally, we relate our findings to the theoretical frameworks of anisotropic chaotic inflation and weak-field solutions, and we provide an updated set of conditions for these models, meeting the requirement of positive Weyl curvature index in an expanding universe. We conclude by highlighting the powerful analytical tools provided by our bivector approach, particularly in solving Einstein's field equations using the Newman-Penrose equations. This bivector method can be adapted to tackle other complex problems in General Relativity, making it a valuable tool for further research in this field. Finally, we correct an earlier mistake in the context of this review, specifically in the equation (49). The correct equation (49) should represent a real electromagnetic field with a self-dual part, instead of being associated with the electromagnetic field in an expanding universe. Similarly, the equation (50) should describe a complex self-dual electromagnetic field in the standard Minkowski space basis, rather than being linked to the electromagnetic field in an expanding universe through conformal coupling. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new technique utilizes linear regression models to generate specific properties in monomer units, which are then combined using an optimized framework based on integer programming. Applying this approach to compounds composed of up to 20 monomers has achieved a level of accuracy comparable to existing polymer models, despite only utilizing a fraction of the potential monomers available in the original framework. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called Dilated Dense Focus Attention Unet, which we applied to data from the CCO dataset. Our research shows that this model can efficiently reduce the required clinical resources while maintaining a high level of accuracy in labeling tumors in the esophagus. To further prove the feasibility of this clinical approach, we selected 20 cases with easily identifiable tumors in the esophagus and asked two experienced radiologists to outline them manually. We found that the precision of our model based on a single training session was significantly better than the precision of experienced radiologists in cases where the outer boundary of the tumors could be seen. However, the precision of the model dropped to around 50% in cases where the tumors had low contrast. To improve the accuracy of the model in such cases, we propose incorporating contextual information from pre-operative endoscopic findings, which we showed could boost the Dice coefficient from 0.45 to 0.60. This augmented model demonstrated its highest level of accuracy in cases with clearly visible tumors and achieved the best results in cases with low contrast, thereby validating the feasibility of the proposed clinical approach. Furthermore, the results of this study are readily applicable in clinical settings. The simplified clinical approach we proposed and the implementation of pre-operative endoscopic information in the model is deemed reliable and efficient in identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus from CT scans. The high precision of the model in cases with easily visible tumors has also been clinically verified. The models we developed and the techniques we proposed for handling difficult cases with low contrast can be used in hospitals immediately. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations, which are often conducted using a limited set of well logs collected during drilling. Real-time formation evaluation and geosteering are also performed with these logs, but the problem of unknown formation properties and log measurements, combined with the influence of uncertainties in these measurements, hinders the accuracy of these processes. This study presents a novel ensemble-based approach that handles uncertain log measurements and unknown formation properties, and is applicable to real-time geosteering and formation evaluation. This method is based on an iterative process that utilizes the ensemble technique, which is normally employed for combining multiple wells, to condition ensembles of models to the uncertain log data collected during drilling. This results in the generation of probability distributions of formation properties, which are derived from the produced models, and indicates how likely it is for the well to be in a particular location within the uncertainty margin. This approach is tested using simulated logs for an actual offshore well, and the generated probability distributions of formation properties are compared to the results obtained with a conventional approach that ignores data from the logging tool that was uncertain. The ensemble approach yielded a broader probability distribution of formation properties, which is more representative of the uncertainty associated with geosteering, and resulted in a higher risk of the well being placed outside the target reservoir. This study demonstrates that log data with a high level of uncertainty can significantly impact the results of formation evaluation and geosteering, which has important implications for the decision-making process. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as parse trees and proposing a novel algorithm to perform nested NER by integrating tree-structured representations. Our experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior or comparable performance compared to state-of-the-art linear models and confirms the benefits of employing tree structures to model nested entities. Furthermore, our method extends standard NER by incorporating hierarchical information, leading to improved performance when limited training data is available. Additionally, our approach facilitates the integration of hierarchical knowledge graph information, resulting in enhanced performance across various evaluation metrics. Our study sets a new direction for standard and nested NER by emphasizing the importance of comprehensive structure parsing. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train image description generation models, which are typically trained using a comparison-based loss function that measures the similarity between generated descriptions and these references. It has been observed that visual description datasets often contain inaccurate or misleading captions, which can lead to models being trained on flawed benchmarks. In response, we propose a novel approach that assesses the validity of reference captions through a reliability metric, which indicates whether a caption is considered accurate or not. In testing our method with a popular dataset, we found that unreliable captions significantly impeded the performance of models, which aligns with expectations. Moreover, our experiment shows that overhauling the dataset by replacing unreliable captions with more trustworthy ones results in substantial improvements in model proficiency. This advancement holds true even when models are trained with other optimization techniques, such as ranking-based objectives. In summary, our findings suggest that using human-generated captions for training are not a requirement and that incorporating a reliability metric, along with a comparison-based loss function, is a more effective way to train visually descriptive models. In addition, our study raises important considerations for both researchers and practitioners who rely on human-generated captions from online sources, as well as those who rely on other types of annotated data, such as labeled classes or object bounding boxes. In response to these concerns, we introduce the Reliability-Paired Dataset Exchange Format (RPDEF), a new standard for releasing and utilizing reliably paired data, along with a leading dataset developed under this guideline. This newly created dataset, alongside our proposed method, outperforms all existing leaderboards and sets a new benchmark for the field. In conclusion, we highlight that both the methodology and results we presented are equally applicable to other domains, such as text-to-text translation. In response to these findings, we invite the research community to contribute to further innovation in this domain. This contribution can take the form of either introducing novel loss functions or exploring alternative approaches to evaluate visually descriptive models. In addition, both practitioners and researchers within the field are warmly invited to join us in developing the Reliability-Paired Dataset Exchange Format (RPDEF), a new standard for releasing and utilizing reliably paired data. This new standard is designed to ensure transparency in both dataset creation and evaluation protocols, ensuring that any findings based on such datasets are both reproducible and comparable. Furthermore, we anticipate that both the method proposed and the newly released dataset will serve as a stepping stone for the development of more advanced techniques, such as generating multiple descriptions for a single image. Previous studies attributed the spread of misinformation to individual factors such as education and media literacy, or the characteristics of specific information campaigns. Conversely, our research suggests that broader structural changes, specifically the Big Sort and Big Move phenomena described by Professor Arthur, play a significant role in the dissemination of misinformation. We based our analysis on a dataset of approximately 100,000 daily submissions and 300,000 comments on Reddit from 2017 to 2020. Our findings indicate that the spread of misinformation correlates strongly with the Big Geographic Shift, experiencing a similar surge during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. A potential explanation for this phenomenon is the idea that internet circulation patterns are influenced by physical mobility patterns, with implications for targeted public health campaigns. We propose a mathematical model representing the interaction between information dissemination and mobility, and verify our predictions through numerical simulations. Our research has important ramifications for the development of effective strategies to contain the spread of misinformation. Next, we plan to refine our model by integrating economic factors and examining the role of third-party influencers. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback, which is readily provided during human-instruction. Understanding the underlying sound patterns of demonstrated tasks can optimize speech-based robot training and make it more effective. However, the difficulty lies in analyzing complex audio signals that result from undetermined task settings and poorly defined task definitions, making it challenging to extract task-specific features. A novel approach is proposed to address this issue by using an automated method to classify demonstrations based on their acoustic structure, eliminating the need for human annotations. Additionally, features learned from speech data are compared to those from demonstration audio, revealing that both contain valuable information for teaching robots. Our findings indicate that audio data from demonstrations contains more task-specific information than speech data from the same speaker, leading to better robot performance when using features learned from demonstration audio. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing system for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. These challenges hinder the development of an effective automated testing system. To illustrate this issue, we present an example of a simple game developed with a Python framework, called Distjo, and demonstrate how the current implementation of automated testing falls short due to these challenges. As a key contribution, we propose a novel approach for comparing the meaning of utterances, taking into account the consequences of their interaction, and demonstrate its efficacy with the earlier mentioned game example. This comparison approach enables the evaluation of conversational systems based on their ability to resolve conflicts arising during interactions with multiple users simultaneously. Unfortunately, as the costs associated with human evaluation are significant, there is a need to incorporate more cost-effective human-or machine-based evaluation methods. To this end, we outline a set of straightforward evaluation guidelines that can be implemented by a human or a machine, and demonstrate how they can be integrated with our automated testing system. This integrated system is capable of handling a variety of dialog management systems, includes multiple test cases, and is efficient in terms of memory usage. To facilitate reproducibility, we have made the source code of our automated testing system publicly available. This system, although initially developed for a simple game, has the potential to be adapted for use with other conversational systems. As a result of incorporating human-or machine-based evaluation methods, we have observed a notable reduction in the number of latent errors present in the system, and have achieved this without experiencing any decline in user engagement. This has been corroborated by both qualitative and quantitative analysis of user interactions with the system. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, we have conducted a systematic evaluation of all test cases, as well as user-generated content, and have observed a marked decrease in the number of previously undetected errors in the system. Using existing data, we analyze the gravitational effect of a hypothetical Planet X on its orbit and its impact on the trajectories of known planets in our solar system. By examining the limitations of general relativity and Newton's laws, we set up a mathematical framework to estimate Planet X's influence. We calculate that its effect would be visible in the movement of Neptune, especially in its semi-major axis and eccentricity. However, the challenge lies in differentiating this gravitational impact from the effects of Neptune's irregular motion. Based on this analysis, we believe that detecting Planet X through its impact on the orbits of the known planets may not be feasible with current technology. Additionally, we find that the traditional method of analyzing planetary movements is sufficient, even when considering the gravitational influence of Planet X. Furthermore, we find that searching for Planet X through its impact on the movement of the known planets results in a lower mass limit, which is significantly higher than the mass limits derived from stellar motions and the motion of the Oort Cloud. This research provides a theoretical framework for validating the existence of Planet X and estimating its characteristics. This framework can also be applied to searching for massive exoplanets. This work is a theoretical examination of the gravitational influence of an unseen planet on the movement of the known planets in our solar system. This study is relevant to the ongoing search for the mysterious Planet X and its characteristics. This paper introduces a novel approach to neural machine translation, incorporating a lexicon memory developed from monolingual data. Unlike auxiliary languages used for training in semi-supervised NMT, the lexicon memory draws upon a vast amount of unsupervised data. It functions as a knowledge base that contains word-level information, allowing the system to draw upon this knowledge during translation. We demonstrate that this model excels in handling unknown words and obscure phrases during translation, and our experiments show that it outperforms standard NMT systems. We also examine the inherent ability of the model to handle general monolingual knowledge and demonstrate its applications in post-processing the generated translations. Our results indicate that this approach yields substantial improvements in data efficiency and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the WMT'14 English-to-French task. Our findings suggest that these techniques can be extended to other low-resource language pairs and may have implications for handling out-of-vocabulary words. We release the code and the pre-trained models used in this study. Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyze the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially find anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies are later dismissed as the features are found to be consistent with simulations involving foreground effects and cosmic structures. Unfortunately, the HawkingNet analysis does not yield statistically significant results to support the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. Moreover, a separate analysis using a different method called Multiresolution Haar Transform also fails to detect the predicted features in the CMB. The study highlights the complexity involved in analyzing the CMB and the importance of cross-verifying results through different techniques. Ultimately, the search for Hawking points and low-variance circles continues as a means to differentiate between the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model and other cosmological models. Additionally, the study reveals that the ability to detect these features relies on the choice of analysis method, underscoring the need for a robust approach that can withstand variations in selection effects. Theoretical models relying on the CMB as evidence must ensure that their predictions align with actual observations, as the haughty claims of discovery do damage to the field as a whole. The name of the study is proposed to be modified to focus on the general concept, thus becoming the Hawking Points and Low Variance Circles Analysis Group. The initiative encourages collaborative analysis among members to explore the possibilities of actually detecting the predicted features in the CMB. A potential member of the analysis group expresses skepticism towards the idea, highlighting that the predicted patterns are based on a specific cosmological model and many open issues remain in the field, as he decides to join the discussion. This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which established the convergence in norm for a class of solutions to the fractional Yamabe flow on compact intervals. The current research expands on that result by relaxing the restriction on initial data, thereby obtaining a broader convergence criterion based on the decay of data near the Yamabe inequality and its relation to the fractional Yamabe equation's energy space. The extension involves introducing a new monotonicity formula related to the fractional Yamabe flow's first variation, which provides a more general inequality than the classical Yamabe inequality and its counterparts in the mean curvature flow and Schrödinger map contexts. The new inequality is relevant to solutions whose conformal scalar curvature changes sign, and it defines a monotone quantity that determines the approach to the Yamabe inequality or its nonexistence. The relaxation of initial data conditions allows for the possibility of singularities under minimal technical assumptions, and it is shown that the closure of the energy space can be reached by solutions whose conformal scalar curvature changes sign in the same manner as smooth solutions whose data decay at a similar rate, thus demonstrating the accessibility of solutions with singularity through flow. The result is a proof of the existence of solutions with conformal scalar curvature changing sign for data in the energy space near zero, and it implies the existence of solutions with singularities for data slightly above the zero energy level, thus providing a new approach to solving the Yamabe equation on manifolds with conformal scalar curvature changing sign. To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for supporting episodes (new categories) often fall short, especially when the number of supporting samples is very low. This paper introduces an original approach that constructs category-specific prototypes using a network trained with a contrastive learning objective, and employs this prototype to recognize new categories in few-shot learning scenarios. The proposed prototype is a representative of the new category that incorporates information from all supporting samples at once, unlike the average prototype of all samples, which does not over-rely on atypical data points with exceptional features. The introduced approach is straightforward, yet effective, and is applied to experiments on miniImageNet, showing that it achieves better results than baseline models and established few-shot learning methods like metric learning and generative models, even when the number of supporting samples is as low as one. The code is available online at https://github.com/zwang84/prototypes. The method is further found to generalize well to real-world applications in transfer learning and domain adaptation. When the number of supporting samples is five or more, the proposed approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods, but often requires significant more parameters than legacy models. This comes with the cost of increased complexity, involving extra parameters and two additional operations over standard few-shot learning methods, specifically cross-domain contrastive loss and query-only forward pass. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the parameters required for different numbers of supporting samples, and finds that the sweet spot for the proposed approach is typically when the number of supporting samples is three. This is attributed to a proposed explanation that average prototypes are robust when the number of supporting samples is very large, but the proposed class-type prototypes are more accurate when the number of supporting samples is between one and ten. This is visually represented with a graph in Figure 1 of the paper. This result is further validated in an extensive set of experiments on miniImageNet, and it is interesting to note that the performance gain of the proposed approach over baseline models and legacy few-shot learning methods increases with smaller supporting samples. This is visually represented with a graph in Figure 2 of the paper. This result raises the possibility that the class-type prototypes may perform better with smaller supporting samples, and this is explored in experiments on miniImageNet with a random split of the data, and it is found that the class-type prototypes outperform baseline models and legacy few-shot learning methods regardless of the specific way the data is split,

We introduce a new challenge in collaborative filtering, where items are categorized into multiple sparse domains, and a recommendation system is tasked with providing personalized suggestions to users across all domains. In practice, a cooperative approach can leverage cross-domain information to enhance item coverage and quality. However, existing methods fall into three limitations: 1) relying on item-based cross-domain connections, which neglects the inherent category structure; 2) using simple linear combinations of cross-domain scores, which underutilizes the rich information within each category; and 3) ignoring the diversity of user preferences across different domains, which can lead to poor performance due to excessive reliance on dense domains. To address these issues, we propose a Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation framework, which incorporates a neighborhood-based method to exploit local relationships within each category and employs a contrastive learning technique to capture the inherent structure of each domain. Additionally, our approach introduces a diversity-promoting component to anticipate user interests across all domains. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, and we publicly release the code and dataset at https://github.com/AlvinGao/MCDCF. With significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, our method achieves a notable 45% boost in New Item Evaluation metric on the Amazon co-purchase dataset and outperforms them by at least 20% on three other cross-domain recommendation datasets. In real-world applications, our proposed framework achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods with moderate increase in computational complexity. Furthermore, we find that our approach achieves practical implications by improving new item coverage and diversity in recommendations. In particular, our method raises new item coverage by up to 24% and diversity by up to 35% across all domains. In real-world scenarios with 50 new items in each domain, our approach takes approximately 2 seconds to make 1000 recommendations. To facilitate further research, we gather empirical data to provide actionable insights for cross-domain recommendation, highlighting the challenge of domain diversity and variability in item density, along with key factors influencing model performance. Lastly, we discover that both item and user diversity play critical roles in maintaining low coverage-to-diversity gaps, while dense domains generally pose a higher challenge than sparse domains. To address these issues, we propose the open research question of exploring different density-aware loss functions to mitigate the limitations of dense domains. Additionally, we plan to investigate further optimization techniques for our proposed framework in the future. Convex optimization issues often take on the form of conic representations, featuring combinations of linear inequalities and fundamental conic inequalities from various families such as semidefinite, exponential cone, or second-order cone inequalities. While some algorithms can directly handle these individual conic inequalities, others can only cope with their combinations. Therefore, an efficient way to work with conic representations involves decomposing them into simpler expressions and then manipulating them into standardized forms acceptable to various solvers. This process can be quite complicated, especially for non-standard conic representations. In this work, we introduce an open-source Julia package named Hypatia, which provides a set of linear, logistic, and exponential cone formulas that can be used to express complex conic formulations in a standardized form. Furthermore, Hypatia offers a variety of its own strong convexity formulas, along with a tool for passing on user-defined functions to a solver. As a result, users can solve complex conic optimization problems with just a few lines of code, without needing to delve into the technical details of how to represent their problem in the required standard form. The code for Hypatia has been made available on GitHub, along with a user guide that outlines available options for passing on additional information to a solver. This feature is particularly useful when working with strong convexity formulas that can be challenging to handle for some solvers. Hypatia has been designed to be compatible with both MOSEK and JuMP. Furthermore, it provides a high-level interface for users to pass on their problem variables, variable bounds, and objective function. This interface allows users to easily modify or extend the capabilities of Hypatia. Additionally, Hypatia includes a performance testing module that enables users to evaluate and compare the performance of different solvers on a given problem. This feature is available under the MIT License. Currently, Hypatia can solve general semidefinite, second-order cone, and exponential cone optimization problems. It can also solve problems involving combinations of these conic inequalities. However, it does not support rotating cone, hermitian matrix cone, or power cone inequalities. Therefore, users may need to express problems involving these conic inequalities in an alternative form using the available linear, logistic, and exponential cone inequalities. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the resilience of power distribution networks, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this phenomenon and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further research into energy systems' multi-dimensional resilience. Keywords: power distribution resilience, private electric vehicles, transportation and energy systems co-optimization, multi-agent optimization, reformation.

Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) offers nonvolatile memory access speeds comparable to DRAM, enabling applications to achieve higher performance and support more transactions. However, the limitations of Optane DC PMM, including capacity, cost, and binary-wise access, may imply that only highly transactional workloads can benefit from it. Yet, actual measurements indicate that many systems can take full advantage of the performance benefits, thanks to the relatively low cost of Optane DC PMM in relation to DRAM. When used as cache, Optane DC PMM can provide 2-3 times better performance than cache hierarchies, and when marshaling data for multiple CPUs, it can handle up to 50,000 IOPS with just 2-3 Optane DC PMMs. Moreover, applications that can benefit from Optane DC PMM include those with sequential access patterns, such as database sorting and batch processing, and even some web applications that can benefit from in-place updates. Finally, while there are some applications that may require custom programming to utilize Optane DC PMM effectively, many others can achieve significant performance gains with minimal or no modifications. As a result, we believe that the performance benefits of Optane DC PMM are more extensive than previously thought, and therefore, we introduce a new category of transactional workloads that are well-suited for the technology. Additionally, we provide various configurations and benchmark results that can serve as a reference for researchers and practitioners alike. Furthermore, we also offer some advice on how to design and implement applications that can efficiently utilize the capabilities of Optane DC PMM. As the first module based on phase-change technology to be integrated into the memory hierarchy, Optane DC PMM may mark the beginning of a new era in memory technology, and its performance benefits may inspire a re-examination of various design choices and optimization techniques that are commonly held as axiomatic. As such, we anticipate that the introduction of more practical and scalable memory technologies will further broaden the range of applications that can benefit from in-place updates and other optimizations that utilize nearby memory locations. Therefore, we propose that the term "high-transaction" workloads be replaced with more descriptive terms such as "transaction-intensive" or "data-intensive" to better capture the essence of the underlying application patterns. Moreover, we also believe that the emergence of more sophisticated memory technologies, such as those described in the Sanjay Kale paper, may lead to a situation where the traditional distinction between cache and main memory becomes less meaningful

Effective collaboration between agents in a meeting scenario depends on the motivation of the agents involved. A new concept called the Drive Theory is introduced, explaining how agents' internal states influence their actions and motivation. A drive-based approach is developed to design a motivation system that responds to changes in the external task environment and internal agent states, promoting optimal performance through personalized motivation techniques and data-driven improvements. This motivation system is integrated with an existing model for collaborative tasks, leading to improved performance and reduced dependencies on external rewards. The proposed approach is evaluated in a scenario involving multiple agents in a recurrent task. Diverse experimentation shows that drive-based motivation leads to better performance, reduced agent exploration, and a more sustainable solution to complex scheduling issues. The results demonstrate the potential of this approach to create more natural and human-like agent interactions. The proposed drive-based mechanism is found to facilitate natural language conversations and improves the robustness of the system in handling various form of agent behavior. The data collected from the experimentation is also analyzed to identify key aspects of the drive-based mechanism. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Additionally, our calculations suggest that the magnetic moment in GdSn3 can be controlled through pressure influences, presenting an alternative method for spintronic technology. Nonetheless, applying pressure may provide an effective means of controlling the magnetic moment in the CmSn3 compound. Our results also indicate that both pressure and lattice distortion can trigger a metal-to-insulator transition in the GdSn3 compound. Our study identifies type-A antiferromagnetism as the most stable magnetic configuration in these materials and highlights the potential of GdSn3 and the GdxCm1-xSn3 series as multifunctional materials. Moreover, we propose that research on phase-pure CmSn3 compounds remains warranted. Lastly, our calculations correlate the magnetic moment reduction in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series with an expansion of the unit cell and the rising atomic volume of the mixed Gd/Cm sites. The HADRON-EFT working group analyzed predictions made by theorists working with effective field theories (EFTs) and lattice QCD for the masses of 16 previously predicted new baryons and mesons. These predictions originated from previous meetings in 2019 and 2020. The working group members submitted their own mass range estimates to the database and reviewed recent publications, ultimately concluding that most newly predicted particles still fall within the range of their expected values. However, the working group noted that certain particles may not be distinguishable from background noise until next-generation experiments with enhanced sensitivity become available. Theoretical interpretations of recent lattice QCD mass predictions for some baryon combinations suggest that they might be resistant to corrections, which could lead to further precise predictions of these combinations' values, potentially increasing the likelihood of their discovery. The database and the discussion held during the meetings are now publicly available. The working group recommends considering observables related to source and decay properties, which could provide additional insight into the search for these particles, and proposes extending the scope of the study to other areas of physics beyond antideuterons, meson-baryon combinations, and strangeness, while also exploring the application of EFT tools to the search for these particles. The working group members are invited to share their research on these additional areas at future meetings. The foundation theorem in the theory of automata and formal languages originates from Chomsky's work on context-free languages. It states that every context-free language contains a subset that corresponds to context-free grammars in a more simplified form. This context-free subset can be generated by deterministic context-free languages, which in turn can be recognized by deterministic pushdown automata. The foundation theorem implies that the language families defined by deterministic pushdown automata and context-free languages are equivalent. This notion of the foundation theorem has been expanded upon in the theory of abstract automata and monoids. Here, we present an extension of the foundation theorem to the B-type Coxeter groups, providing a theoretical basis for the connection between deterministic pushdown automata and context-free languages within this more general framework. This involvement of the B-type Coxeter groups renders the foundation theorem independent of the ordering of generators and words, as well as allowing for a more nuanced view of the intersection and union operations in context-free languages. The proof of the foundation theorem for the B-type Coxeter groups relies on the properties of the order relation and word order in these groups, and demonstrates that these groups serve as a universal framework for determining the context-free nature of languages. Furthermore, this theory can be applied to resolve some long-standing open problems and conjectures in the field of context-free languages. The name "foundation theorem" may be seen as a tribute to the significant influence that Chomsky's work has had on the development of the theory of abstract automata and monoids. Additionally, we provide a historical account of the foundation theorem and its extensions within the context of formal languages and abstract automata, highlighting the key contributions of various researchers over the years. This includes a discussion on the connection between context-free languages and deterministic pushdown automata, as well as the more general language families defined by deterministic parity automata and counter automata. By stacking VRFM on top of the traditional detector framework, we achieve notable improvements in accuracy on challenging benchmarks like VOC 2012. By analyzing listings and waiting times for all patients, as well as the characteristics of available donations, a set of algorithms can identify the most beneficial recipients to prioritize. However, this approach raises concerns about fairness, as patients with higher waiting times may be given lower priority over time. Additionally, the system's reliance on complex models and sophisticated computation methods can create barriers to entry for smaller organ procurement agencies. This paper presents a new approach to optimal acceptance, one that is simpler, more flexible, and easier to understand and implement. By replacing the intricate models with more basic rules, this system aims to provide a fair and practical solution to the challenge of matching kidney donations with recipients. Through simulation testing, this new approach is shown to be just as effective as the more complex systems, but with several key advantages. The paper also explores potential applications to other transplant matches, such as livers and corneas, and discusses the role of patient preferences in the matching process. The new approach is now being put into use by the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) in conjunction with the new waitlist management system. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to learn relevant information from these examples. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address this issue, we introduce an enhanced version of the word2vec model, aimed at separating the implicit distribution of co-occurring words from the explicit meaning of words. Our experiments demonstrate the advantages of this enhanced model in tasks like text classification and the prediction of absolute prices. Moreover, it demonstrates lower non-stationarity in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names over time. Our research provides a thorough mathematical understanding of the word2vec model, highlighting its limitations and potential applications in addressing the challenges associated with NLP embeddings. Our study on financial NLP embeddings serves as a precedent for researchers to revisit their models in light of the underlying structure of the data they are analyzing. Our results also emphasize the value of using financial datasets, given the unique characteristics of financial corpora that distinguish them from other datasets. Our research on the word2vec model paves the way for the exploration of alternative implementations of the Skip-gram learning method, prompting researchers to examine the influence of the implicit structure of corporate datasets on the generation of word2vec embeddings. By leveraging either a SISO-OFDM or MISO-OFDM structure, these systems aim to minimize the total time and transmit power, subject to an energy harvesting constraint, in a multi-user scenario. To accelerate policy optimization in continuous control tasks, experience replay is an effective technique by reusing previously collected data. However, using the original formulation of ER straightforwardly may lead to suboptimal results due to several issues. On one hand, the variance of target policy affects sampling efficiency, with a poorly designed target network resulting in inconsistent data quality. On the other hand, the variance of the value function estimates, arising from both the target and the critic networks, causes sampling noise, reducing the efficacy of optimization. Presently, an enhanced experience replay framework, named Variance Diminution based Experience Replay (VDER), is introduced to address these challenges. The proposed method reduces the variance of the target policy and value function estimates through network optimization, thereby minimizing the discrepancy between the target and the critic networks. As a result, VDER yields a more consistent data distribution, enabling more efficient optimization of the policy. The advantages of VDER are exemplified through superior performance on benchmark continuous control tasks, showcasing notable improvements over basic ER and policy gradient methods. I'd like to introduce libcommute, a versatile C++11/14/17 template library that makes it easy to work with polynomial operators used in the quantum many-body theory by creating a specialized dialect for the Mathematica symbol language. Additionally, it serves as a comprehensive toolkit for the development of exact diagonalization codes, closely mirroring the functionality of in-house group tools. In its current form, the Mathematica interface is the primary front-end for interacting with the library, although other potential interfaces are also being considered. Key features of the library are its ability to efficiently compute commutators, perform unitary transformations, and construct operator expectations, all of which are fundamental components for developing exact diagonalization methods. Furthermore, it provides an intuitive way to define and utilize quantum states, including various common spin and boson field states, and includes tools for the eigenvalue problem solution, such as finding eigenenergies and constructing matrices that project onto eigenstates. Moreover, libcommute enables easy data export to MATLAB and C++/Eigen, making it an extremely useful library for any project involving the quantum many-body theory. Our studies uncover a distinct correlation between the spin lattice relaxation and electrical conductivity, revealing a sharp increase in spin lattice relaxation in proportion to the square of conductivity. This relationship indicates that the spin lattice relaxation is a direct measure of the charge carrier density, allowing us to utilize $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR as a nonlocal probe of the electron liquidity in these systems. Notably, the resistivity of the LaNiO$_3$ layer dominates the overall proportionality, suggesting that the LaAlO$_3$ layer has a negligible impact on the spin lattice relaxation in this context. Moreover, our findings indicate that the resistivity of the LaNiO$3$ layer is intrinsically linear with temperature, in contrast to previous results which reported a temperature-independent resistivity for this layer. We propose that the underlying cause of this discrepancy lies in the varying levels of strain experienced by the LaNiO$3$ layer in different superlattices, with a $5$ unit layer being the least constrained and exhibiting the most pronounced linear behavior.
