Our research enhances a recent study on the performance of wireless networks that use intelligent surface technology by considering two important factors: correlation among antenna elements and the distortion of phase-shifting. We investigate these aspects, which are often overlooked in research, by developing an efficient method for calculating the rate of data transfer across multiple signals. We then determine the conditions under which the maximum data transfer rate is achieved and establish an upper limit for it. Furthermore, we find the condition under which the data transfer rate is stable across different transmissions and derive the average data transfer rate. Finally, we validate our analytical findings with a network that has multiple signal paths and show that it can achieve a high data transfer rate of about 90% of the theoretical maximum. We also compare different techniques for transferring data across multiple signals and find that our analytical method is more accurate than a recently proposed model. Overall, our study provides valuable insights into the performance of wireless networks that use intelligent surfaces and can help optimize their design. We investigate how the transfer rate of a multi-antenna, intelligent-surface-assisted wireless network can be optimized. First, we establish the minimum requirement for achieving the highest possible transfer rate and determine its maximum value, taking into account signal interference and the requirement that the transmitted and received signals carry the same information. We find that the highest possible transfer rate is at least half as much as the lowest frequency of the transmitted and received signals, and this rate decreases proportionally with increasing signal interference. We also find that there is a maximum limit to how much the transfer rate can be improved with multiple receiving antennas, and this limit is achieved when the transmitted and received signals carry the same information and have the highest possible similarity in terms of the information they carry. We then determine the condition under which the transfer rate is stable across different transmissions and show that this condition is met when the transmitted and received signals carry the same information and have the highest possible similarity in terms of the information they carry. We derive the average transfer rate as the transfer rate multiplied by the probability of it being achievable, and we show that this probability increases with multiple receiving antennas when the transmitted and received signals carry the same information and have the highest possible similarity in terms of the information they carry. We validate our analytical findings using a network that has multiple signal paths and show that it can achieve a high transfer rate of about 90% of the theoretical maximum, and this requires careful optimization of the design of the transmitted and received signals to carry the same information and have the highest possible similarity in terms of the information they carry

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific class of systems, characterized by relaxing consistency for better scalability and responsiveness, can leverage conflict-free replicated data structures (CRDDS). However, the design of such systems is hindered by the difficulty of producing parallelizable code for existing implementations. To address this limitation, we present Remove-Win, a novel design framework for CRDDS. By separating the update operation into successor and winner determination components, Remove-Win enables both parts to be optimized independently. This distinction enables the development of highly efficient, low-latency implementations for updates, regardless of the underlying graph structure. To demonstrate the flexibility of Remove-Win, we create multiple CRDDS using various winner determination algorithms, resulting in significant performance improvements over existing replicated data structures. Furthermore, our benchmark tests show that in-memory systems using Remove-Win-based data structures exhibit sub-second latency for both small and large datasets. Additionally, our framework facilitates the creation of systems that can tolerate up to three concurrent updates and reduce tail latency, achieving a 5.5 times overall performance improvement over a baseline in-memory system. To validate the feasibility of Remove-Win in practice, we develop and test an in-memory document-store system, demonstrating that it can survive up to three concurrent updates and reduce tail latency by 42.3%. Our framework and the document-store system are open-sourced and available for use. Additionally, we present two additional use cases for Remove-Win, including a key-value store and a hybrid store combining both types. These implementations highlight the versatility of our design framework, making it suitable for a wide range of applications and use cases. By leveraging Remove-Win, developers can create efficient, scalable, and high-performance systems for real-time web applications and other demanding workflows. Our design framework and implementations provide a proven solution for building reliable and responsive systems, enabling developers to produce working prototypes and functional systems with minimal code and rapid development cycles. Our analysis reveals the shocks' fast motion through the star's envelope is slowed down by accumulating matter, eventually becoming opaque to electromagnetic radiation due to the envelope's heating, whereas in core-collapse explosions, this opacity barrier is overcome by the high initial energy release. Similar to supernovae with newly formed black holes or neutron stars, we find that shocks from stellar eruptions can also generate fast-moving matter along the axis of symmetry and a globally expanding envelope located behind the shock's rear. These characteristics, along with energy distributions and light curves, match recent observations of two stars thought to have experienced supernovae, specifically SN 2000es and SN 2010mc. Our study indicates that shocks from stellar eruptions can result in massive amounts of matter being accelerated to high velocities, potentially contributing to the fast-moving matter component and a globally expanding envelope. Recent advances in large-language models have given rise to substantial progress in natural language inference tasks. These models excel at resolving the implied relationships between sentences, as expressed through entailed, contradicted, or neutral labels. Conversely, they struggle to grasp the implicit semantic meanings underlying the sentences, making it challenging for them to generalize across diverse sentence formulations. This study acknowledges the semantic richness inherent in language and seeks to enlarge the scope of natural language inference to incorporate these subtle semantic differences. By constructing new datasets that capture these variations in semantics and testing the existing models' ability to navigate this expanded semantic landscape, our findings highlight the limitations of current models and indicate that there is significant potential for improving the consistency across natural language inference tasks. Moreover, we observe that these models often confuse each other when predicting implied relationships between sentences, resulting in a decrease in performance when comparing the predictions made by different models for the same implicit relationship. This potential for improvement is further validated by the poor results achieved by models that perform exceptionally well on natural language inference tasks but fail to grasp the semantic nuances when applying this knowledge to more complex dialogues. This insight suggests that there is a valuable opportunity to enhance the capability of natural language inference models by incorporating the implicit semantic meanings that are inherent in language and to explore the interplay between these semantic variations and the labels used in natural language inference. This opportunity is particularly significant when considering applications that involve dialogue, where the implicit semantic relationships play a critical role in determining the appropriateness of generated text. This problem is illustrated through the construction of three new datasets that capture the semantic flavors in language and the difficulty models have in predicting these variations when they rely heavily on lexical overlap. This difficulty results in a performance decline when comparing the predictions made by different models for the same implicit relationship, or what we refer to as the semantic variation factor. This factor exerts a significant influence on the predictions made by the models, exceeding the effect of any dataset-specific biases. This influence is particularly pronounced when considering the results achieved by models that perform exceptionally well on natural language inference tasks but fail to grasp the semantic nuances when applying this knowledge to more complex dialogues. A key challenge in developing safe and efficient autonomous driving systems is the ability to identify potential hazards during a critical phase of the driving process - the lane change maneuver. To enhance road safety, it's essential to recognize hazardous actions that occur before a collision can happen. However, the success of this feature depends on the detection of a specific event - which is the lane change action itself. In this research paper, a novel approach to recognizing hazardous actions within video clips of lane changes is proposed. The proposed method focuses on the detection of the start and end points of a lane change action, as well as the classification of harmful actions into three categories: 'dangerous','severe', and 'normal'. To validate the performance of the proposed system, experimental results are reported, indicating that the method achieves impressive accuracy levels - 92.51% for start point detection, 88.73% for end point detection, and 92.11% for harmful action classification. Notably, the method demonstrates exceptional robustness when tested against a diverse set of lane change videos, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models through its integration of a convolutional neural network and Long Short-Term Memory layers, along with a segmentation mask transfer mechanism. In essence, the proposed system is an advanced spatiotemporal model that leverages a driver assistance feature, providing a reliable solution for the recognition of hazardous actions during a critical phase of the driving process - the lane change maneuver. In order to demonstrate the practical applicability of the proposed system, a prototype vehicle integration module was developed, along with instructions for its implementation. In conclusion, the method offers a precise and safe approach for the recognition of harmful actions within video clips of lane changes. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with significant rotations, considering the effects of both the addition of centrifugal force and the potential for break-up, up to a point where mass is lost due to spin. This research focuses on models with masses between 0.9 and 0.7 solar masses and extension times of up to 10 million years. It considers various initial egg shapes, from slightly oblong to greatly elongated, and found that moderate oblong shapes result in stars that burn hydrogen most efficiently. These stars experience hydrogen depletion fastest when rotating the fastest allowed, losing hydrogen in 20 million years, and will have burned about half of their hydrogen supply when this occurs. Very low-mass stars that rotate rapidly lose hydrogen quickly, meeting the criteria for pulsating, slowly rotating stars known as GW Vir stars. This suggests that GW Vir stars should always be rotating at the fastest allowed speed. These stars start in shapes that are greatly elongated, but this shape is unstable and the shape becomes moderate oblong, retaining this shape stability. This stability makes GW Vir stars more resistant to changes caused by gradual slowing down. It also continuously loses mass on its side and at its ends, but this shape can naturally readjust to a more moderate oblong, regaining stability. This paper examines the challenge of incremental learning where the data distribution changes significantly, specifically the issue of learning from domains with highly imbalanced class distributions. Current approaches in this domain focus on developing algorithms that accommodate shifting class imbalances, but without addressing the problem of learning from new classes in future domains. In contrast, our research targets the more complex task of incorporating new classes from domains with significantly different imbalanced patterns. To facilitate this, we assume that the code for new classes remains unchanged. To address this problem, we propose an initial method called CILBI, which introduces a calibrated version of the new classes based on a small amount of labeled data. To evaluate our approach, we conduct comprehensive experiments comparing it to alternative methods of processing future classes. These methods include transferring knowledge from an existing class with a similar name, ignoring new classes unless they are similar to existing ones, and using a pre-trained model. These experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over these baseline methods. Furthermore, we discover that the performance gain of our approach is particularly noticeable when the new classes are significantly different from the old ones. To better understand the challenges of this problem, we also conduct an in-depth analysis of the category confusion issue. This problem refers to the situation where a single new class corresponds to multiple previous classes with different imbalanced patterns. To handle this challenge, we propose an approach called CILBI-Cl, which involves clustering the data from the new domain based on the data from the old domains. This approach allows us to calculate the distribution of classes within each cluster and use this information to calibrate the model. To validate our approach, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the category confusion issue using both theoretical and simulation-based methods. These methods demonstrate the potential of our approach to handle complex class confusion issues. Currently, the energy spent on frequency changes is proportional to the number of cores and the frequency square, which is extremely high. We investigate whether the Higgs boson could be responsible for the recently reported discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, with the Higgs mass ranging from its known value to as high as 1 TeV. To determine this, we perform a comprehensive assessment of all major contributions which involve the Higgs boson and its interactions with heavy quarks and third-generation vector bosons. Our analysis indicates that a Higgs mass between 250 GeV and 1 TeV could plausibly explain the anomaly, with the Higgs' contribution accounting for nearly all of the predicted discrepancy when its mass exceeds 1.4 TeV. However, it should be noted that a Higgs mass in this range would deviate significantly from the Standard Model's predicted value using its given parameters, with a Higgs parameter point that yields a mass of around 1.3 TeV already being excluded by existing global fits. Our study also reveals that future experiments at DA$\Phi$NE and Higgs factories could confirm or dismiss a Higgs-related explanation as early as the mid-2020s. Moreover, we find that the Higgs' influence on the muon's magnetic moment is highly sensitive to the value of the top-quark's effective electroweak parameter, with its determination becoming increasingly accurate with ongoing top-quark depth studies. As a result, we advocate for continued attention to be paid to this sector, with it being crucial for a comprehensive, anomaly-driven probe of the Standard Model's consistency. Furthermore, we highlight that identifying the Higgs as the source of the discrepancy would have far-reaching implications, with it being consistent with our understanding of the Higgs' role in the Standard Model and its breaking mechanism, while it would also imply the existence of a non-zero effective top-yukawa coupling in the electroweak sector. Additionally, it would result in a significant contribution from the Higgs integral, with it being in line with our knowledge of the Higgs' properties derived from its discovery at the Large Hadron Collider. Our study paves the way for a deeper investigation of the Higgs' interactions, with it being of utmost importance that the predicted DA$\Phi$NE and Higgs factory sensitivities are achieved in the near future. We conclude by highlighting that the Higgs could matter significantly for the anomaly, with it being the most compelling explanation on offer, while it is also the most sensitive to experimental feedback, with it being the best scientific motive for continuing to push the boundaries of what is possible with precision physics

We explore how the server's model influence can be exploited and how participant data is at risk due to inadequate encryption and learning techniques. We also investigate the exchange of sensitive information between participants and the server's abuse of their trust. We stress the need for robust security measures to protect participants' privacy and encourage further research into the development of practical privacy-preserving methods for vertical federated learning. Additionally, we outline a simple encryption method called'model encryption' and invite researchers to build upon our findings through further investigation of practical privacy assaults on vertical federated learning. We have released our findings as an open-source paper to facilitate such development. Moreover, we have established a starting point for the creation of a benchmark to assess the performance of various privacy-preserving vertical federated learning protocols. The primary aim in Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a polysemous word based on its context within a larger text.  Context-dependent polysemy, the most prevalent form of WSD, occurs when a word's meaning shifts in response to changes in its surrounding context.  Given the endless possibilities of word combinations in language, each word's sense becomes unique based on the combination of words it is used with, effectively making the WSD task all-encompassing.  Given the inherent difficulty of automating this process, much research has focused on developing methods to assist in resolving contextual ambiguity.  One such approach, represented by the model introduced in Huang et al. ("GlossBERT: A Data-driven Bottom-up Framework for Word Sense Disambiguation") paper, employs a data-driven method to present words with multiple senses using a context-independent representation.  By combining the introduced GlossBERT framework with a context-dependent extension, we demonstrate the potential for significant enhancements in performing WSD tasks.  Specifically, we report notable improvements over baseline models and the current state-of-the-art approaches on three distinct datasets, achieving up to a 24.5% point increase in SAW score, following the introduction of word ambiguity.  Moreover, we observe the model's ability to generalize beyond training data, resulting in outstanding performance even in situations with longer context sentences and multiple unknown words.  The introduced model also outperforms the existing word similarity baselines while achieving a 49.4% increase in semantic relatedness score on the BERT-based coefficient calculator.  The introduced framework's effectiveness is further validated through the evaluation of a word ambiguity dataset created in conjunction with the model, producing accurate results compared to those obtained through human annotations. However, the presence of word ambiguity still results in lower SAW scores than the baseline scores, indicating that there is room for further improvement. A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Our study also demonstrates that the resonant frequency-based attack can target multiple rooms simultaneously. Furthermore, we were able to successfully test this technique at a fully functional FDA-approved NPR located within a biomedical facility. Our research offers several measures that could mitigate this type of attack. We believe that this threat highlights the need for closer collaboration between bio-safety experts, infectious-control practitioners, and audio signal processing specialists. Our study provides a new perspective on the unique challenges posed by contemporary bio-safety containment facilities. We have proposed the term "hidden threat" to describe this type of danger, where the malicious audio represents a concealed path to compromising the containment facilities. Our study has paved the way for further exploration into the concept of hidden threats and it has defined a framework that can be applied across multiple disciplines. Our research has demonstrated that resonant frequency-based attacks can successfully evade detection by modern automated security systems, thereby creating a new paradigm for predicting and preventing threats to containment facilities. Our study has provided a new definition for predicting potential threats, which is based on the unique acoustic characteristics of a room. We have proposed a new protocol for monitoring potential threats, which takes into account the unique acoustic characteristics of a room. Our study has demonstrated that this protocol can effectively identify potential threats, which could not be detected by the building management systems. Our research has shown that this protocol can be implemented using existing technology, which makes it a feasible solution. A key characteristic of decentralized energy markets is the presence of storage, which enables reverse flows and allows for the mitigation of bottlenecks in high-demand areas. Considering a multi-period model with various locations and participants, we analyze how risk-averse system operators allocate storage across different locations. Using an Iid independence approximation, we derive a sonderpiece of linear decision problems representing optimized storage allocation strategies in each period. These independent problems capture the effects of being risk-averse and take into account the implications of reverse flows on supply and demand at individual locations. We also introduce an indication of the total storage allocation efficiency loss due to risk aversion, providing a metric to gauge the impact on system performance. Through numerical simulations with various locations and time periods, we show that the independence approximation holds closely, resulting in nearly full storage allocation efficiency even in scenarios with significant bottlenecks, locations, and time periods. Notably, the risk-averse storage allocation outperforms a risk-neutral approach in our tests, indicating the former can yield better overall system performance. The analysis highlights the practical benefits of model simplicity, enabling the use of established algorithms for obtaining approximate solutions. To demonstrate the feasibility of our results, we present a specific use case based on real-world data. The risk-averse formulation requires around 500 milliseconds to compute on a single CPU core, comparable to the 700 milliseconds for a larger-scale risk-neutral model, underscoring the manageable complexity of this approach. The code is available for reproduction of our findings. In time-division duplexing (TDD) systems, individual uplink and downlink time slots are alternatingly scheduled, which can cause imbalances in the quality of service (QoS) for uplink and downlink applications due to the nature of TDD scheduling. For this reason, the scheduling of TDD is more complicated than in frequency-division duplexing (FDD) systems, which do not experience such QoS imbalances. We propose an approach called the game-theoretic model scheduler (GTS) to dynamically optimize TDD scheduling in 5G systems, which allows for efficient balancing of uplink and downlink transmissions in real-time while complying with system constraints and meeting the minimum QoS requirements for applications. Simulations show that the proposed GTS method can adapt quickly to changing conditions and reduce the QoS delays experienced by applications, when compared to static TDD scheduling approaches, which can result in severe QoS delays under certain system load conditions. Additionally, the proposed method achieves similar system spectral efficiency as static TDD scheduling methods, which is in line with 5G system expectations. Which indicates that the GTS method is an effective solution for mitigating the QoS issues associated with TDD systems, which could also be applicable to other time-sliced systems, such as time-sliced frequency-sensing systems. Results showed that the height of the Hall anomaly varied proportionally with the normal state conductivity, displaying a similar dependence on temperature as the vortex resistance. This relationship led to a temperature-dependent voltage value, at which the Hall anomaly became distinct. In this work, we introduce a novel neural network called the Hamiltonian Neural Network, which infers derivatives given past data points. Unlike conventional neural networks that rely on explicit input-output relationships, this model utilizes internal dynamics to capture derivative information. We test the Hamiltonian Neural Network on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that it effectively learns to utilize its internal state to predict outputs from new data points, and that it can learn derivative patterns without being trained on the data explicitly. Additionally, we find that the Hamiltonian Neural Network's performance is comparable to that of traditional neural networks when data points are widely spaced, and that it excels in scenarios where there are missing data points or partial observations. We also apply the Hamiltonian Neural Network to time series data, showing that it can learn to make accurate predictions about future data points. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Despite significant progress in recent years, the majority of methods have focused on utilizing the surrounding words as sources of information, often ignoring other crucial components of the text context.  One underexploited resource in this regard is the glossary provided for each word sense in a lexical database such as WordNet.  Our novel proposal involves a method to select and refine the most relevant context and glosses to improve the disambiguation performance.  This approach is tested on the SEME dataset with multiple senses and results show that it achieves better performance than existing state-of-the-art methods.  Furthermore, our method is found to be effective even with limited training data.  To facilitate the exploration of contextual effects on WSD, a comparative study is also conducted to highlight the diversity of factors influencing the model's performance.  Source code is available at https://github.com/lewis17/ContextGloss.  Our method places third in the SEME WIN WIN competition with an F-score of 57.58%.  In contrast to other top-performing methods, our approach focuses on the context-gloss relationship rather than relying on intricate neural architectures or extensive training.  However, it is worth noting that simple models like the one employed in this study are not compliant with current neural architecture benchmarks.  To address this issue, we modify our model to include a bidirectional transformer encoder and a score calculator, which yields an improvement in F-score to 60.23%.  This enhanced version ranks first in the SEME WIN WIN competition.  Due to the complexity of this improved model, it is no longer considered a simple baseline.  Notably, our method demonstrates that both context and gloss are crucial components of the text that can be leveraged to address the word sense disambiguation task.  Although the current implementation of our approach relies on a pre-trained language model, it is possible to train the context-gloss calculator along with the mask-based score calculator as a whole, which further simplifies the model.  This variant is found to perform on par with the state-of-the-art models that employ multi-task fine-tuning.  On the other hand, our method offers the advantage of being substantially smaller in terms of model size.  This model variant places second in the SEME WIN WIN competition with an F-score of 60.44. The detection of top quark production in proton-lead collisions is a key challenge due to the dense experimental environment resulting from heavy ion collisions. To aid detection, a new set of features is proposed that focuses on differentiating top quark production from minimum bias events. Specifically, it is proposed to utilize properties of top quark decay products, namely the correlation between the momentum of the top quark and the transverse momentum of the dilepton pair. Furthermore, it is suggested that top quark production can be identified by comparing the distribution of the dilepton pair's transverse momentum in proton-lead and proton-proton collisions. Numerical estimates for the sensitivity of these methods at the LHC are also provided. With increasing integrated luminosity, detection becomes feasible at next-generation hadron colliders despite production rates significantly lower than those observed in proton-proton collisions. In contrast, even with very high integrated luminosities, detection may not be possible at current heavy ion colliders. Consequently, detection of top quark production in proton-lead collisions can serve as a strategic test for the capability of heavy ion detectors in detecting rare signals in dense environments. Furthermore, it is proposed that top quark production can be studied in proton-nucleus collisions at future heavy ion colliders with integrated luminosities exceeding $100\,{\text fb}^{-1}}$ provided the detector can efficiently reject background events and accurately calculate the top quark production cross-section, which would provide valuable information on the mass of the top quark in a proton-nucleus background, complementary to measurements obtained in proton-proton collisions. In addition, it is proposed that top quark production can be used as a strategic beam monitor, with measurements correlated to the average number of protons per bunch and therefore potentially sensitive to proton misburn effects and variations in proton bunch populations. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic interpretation, specifically table selection and column selection, as well as the value filling task. Existing work relies heavily on neural-based table filling systems, but we contend that separate neural networks for each task are inadequate. We introduce a novel, unified end-to-end framework that employs neural networks to model all tasks simultaneously. Additionally, to enhance the ability of our model to generalize across domains, we introduce two auxiliary tasks. In experiments using the Spider cross-domain text-to-SQL benchmark, our results indicate that our unified framework outperforms domain-specific baselines while achieving comparable performance to domain-adaptive models without the need for domain-specific training. Moreover, our method demonstrates strong application potential in real-world scenarios through the inclusion of an additional experiment involving a real-world use case. Source code is available at https://github.com/ASAI-HKU/XDT2SQL.

Researchers have been attempting to link two distinct descriptions of interacting Bose gases: one based on first-principles many-body quantum mechanics and another rooted in classical hydrodynamics. A recent study suggests that these two descriptions are interconnected, and this connection can be expressed in terms of a specific relationship involving the Wigner function. This relationship serves as a quantum extension of the hydrodynamic equation known as the quantum hydrodynamic equation. It allows researchers to directly obtain the quantum hydrodynamic equation from first-principles quantum mechanics and establishes a link between the Wigner function and quantum hydrodynamic equation. This approach proves particularly useful for interpreting the outcomes of recent experiments aimed at verifying the quantum hydrodynamics of $^{87}$Rb atoms. Furthermore, this study indicates that the phase-space average of the quantum hydrodynamic equation yields a non-linear equation that is free from ultraviolet divergences and is suitable for predicting macroscopic observables. This averaged equation demonstrates a level of similarity with the Hartree-Fock equation, albeit it differs in its underlying assumption concerning the coherence length and provides a more coherent description of the coherence properties of the system. This study provides valuable insights into the legitimacy and approximate accuracy of this phase-space averaged equation, and it highlights the distinct roles that quantum fluctuations and interactions play in determining the behavior of the system. This understanding gains particular relevance in the face of emerging experiments that will soon be able to scrutinize the internal structure of Bose gases. These experiments involve manipulating the coherence length through the use of optical traps, a feature that will serve as an indicator of the phase-space averaged equation's performance. Nonetheless, due to the fact that quantum fluctuations dominate the behavior of Bose gases even at very low temperatures, it is clear that a classical hydrodynamic approach is insufficient, and a quantum extension becomes necessary. This study provides a foundation for exploring the connection between quantum fluctuations, stated in the Big Sky Theory, and the phase-space averaged equation. This connection holds the key to a deeper understanding of how coherence and quantum fluctuations influence the behavior of interacting Bose gases. This study offers a starting point for delving into the implications of these findings for other quantum systems that involve interparticle interactions and are in motion. This includes, but is not limited to, quantum gases within rotating or gravitationally influenced environments, as well as effects such as gravity and Coriolis forces that induce fluctuations and related hydrodynamic phenomena. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. This metric enables a direct comparison of fuzzers, even if they generate test cases of differing sizes. We validate the efficacy of this approach by conducting a comprehensive analysis of 18 leading fuzzers, covering various techniques and categories, and apply it to identify the most efficient fuzzer for each program under test. Our evaluation also indicates that no single fuzzer consistently outperforms the others across all programs and scenarios, highlighting the importance of carefully selecting a fuzzer for a particular program. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. A critical limitation has hindered this process: until now, it hasn't been feasible to execute an exact calculation due to the enormous number of permutations, despite advancements in computing power. By devoting significant resources to calculating all possible permutations, we have determined the optimal approach to take; we have also optimized a recent algorithm for even greater efficiency. Our method can now yield extremely precise results with a reasonable runtime. For example, even at a 0.01 significance level and 0.95 confidence, we can compute all permutations in under 24 hours on a single GPU. This achievement paves the way for a high degree of confidence in test results and P-values. We have incorporated our approach into two well-known test sets used in the 2020 ConVOI Challenge, and our results indicate that previously achieved performance improvements are likely genuine. We have also developed an open-source implementation of our technique, which has been integrated into the popular Glue-PIAN issue annotator. This tool can now accurately determine whether a system's performance difference is significant or not, based on various criteria, including whether it affects low-frequency events or produces inconsistent results in paired tests. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on the ease of deployment for the loads themselves. This paper proposes a solution where a large number of individually flexible loads, without the need for explicit feedback, can cooperate to convey a similar level of flexibility at a significantly reduced measurement cost. The loads accomplish this by participating in an online learning process that adapts to their actual energy-related costs and enables them to make decisions within a centralized optimization framework that can manipulate the loads' flexible behavior. A theoretical analysis along with simulations demonstrates the advantages of this joint approach, showcasing reduced measurement costs and improved overall flexibility. Furthermore, the scheme is found to be computationally efficient and less complex than other learning-based methods. It also offers a simple mechanism for incentivizing participation, one that could be explored further in the economic context. The implementation of this concept is also discussed in relation to an actual smart grid project. The code used for the experiments is publicly available. The proposed solution yields a simpler implementation and lower measurement costs than other learning-based methods, reducing the complexity by a factor of ten in terms of parameters and half in terms of updates. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ggrosseto/AF-ICO. The actual implementation in the grid is discussed in more detail in Reference \cite{grosseto2021practical}. The resulting system was tested in a real-world setting with over one thousand devices participating over a wireless network link with an average data transfer of 1.5 Kbps, suggesting that the scheme can be viable even in the presence of substantial communication constraints. The practical implications and potential for further improvement are also explored. The modified scheme that handles measurement errors resulted in an increase of less than 5% in the total flexibility compared to the ideal case, indicating that the scheme is robust enough to accommodate some level of measurement errors. The same feedback mechanism can also be applied to other forms of flexible loads such as thermal or mechanical ones. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions for the proposed approach. The paper has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Control of Network Systems as an extended version of our previous publication \cite{grosseto2019af}. The extended version includes additional experimental results, a more comprehensive analysis of the scheme, and a deeper exploration of the theoretical aspects. The paper has been accepted for presentation at the 2020 IEEE

To streamline envelope simulations and reduce burdens on the solver, we introduce SCATTER, a novel envelope formulation that eliminates the need for complex equations and iterations. SCATTER is a unified formalism that encompasses previous models, including the established TOGNINI and HATCHER formulations. Our implementation of SCATTER in the GIZMO code leads to a significant improvement in performance, reducing pair-wise interactions by approximately 30% and improving bridge detection by incorporating velocity information, which results in a 5-fold decrease in bridge formation compared to the standard HATCHER model. Despite these improvements, SCATTER shows negligible differences in substructure formation, galaxy morphology, and rotation curves. Furthermore, we find that the new formalism reduces field particle noise by approximately 20% in massive galaxy systems. Additionally, we observe minimal changes in galaxy properties when comparing simulations using the standard HATCHER model and those using SCATTER, indicating that SCATTER is robust and reliable. Our research highlights the potential of SCATTER to improve the performance of envelope simulations while maintaining the accuracy of the HATCHER model. This study investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on unknown Higgs interactions. We examine two EFTs: the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) and the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT), considering the relevant low-energy effects up to the TeV scale. Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two major detector configurations at CLIC and ILC, incorporating radiative corrections and kinematic selections, to determine the sensitivity to new Higgs couplings. Comparing our findings with existing LHC results, we find that future $e^+e^-$ colliders have the potential to significantly improve current understanding of Higgs physics, with a comprehensive interpretation of results across all available channels being essential. In the case of CLIC operating at 3 TeV and 5 TeV, the sensitivity to the top-quark topological contact interactions is already reached at the TeV scale, while ILC at 1 TeV and 1.2 TeV can match this level of sensitivity in certain channels only, with several dominated by the $b\bar{b}$ channel. In the case of the HEFT operator characterizing a Higgs self-interaction, both CLIC and ILC can reach the TeV scale already at 1 TeV, whereas for the top-sees-top operator, ILC at 1.2 TeV is required to reach the TeV scale in most channels. Our study highlights that $e^+e^-$ colliders have unique advantages in studying the Higgs sector, offering a compelling case for further research into the feasibility of sensitive experiments at these facilities. In addition, we provide detailed predictions and event characteristics for double Higgs production, which can serve as a benchmark for simulations and sensitivity analyses in the context of EFTs, as well as in explorations of new physics beyond the Standard Model. This study also raises important considerations for the development of dedicated experimental strategies, together with a thorough reinterpretation of future collider data within the framework of EFTs. While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityEvaluation is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality assessment tasks and obtain accurate and verifiable quality indicators.  This distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible configuration and adaptive handling of memory constraints, ensuring reliable and performance-oriented evaluation results even with extremely large datasets.  To validate its performance, DistQualityEvaluation was subjected to exhaustive experiments using real-world and synthetic datasets, showcasing its superiority over existing methods and benchmark tools.  The implementation of DistQualityEvaluation has been successfully applied to evaluate the quality of large-scale biomedical datasets, and the framework is freely available for download at its dedicated repository.  Furthermore, a preliminary version of this work was presented at the 12th International Conference on Semantic Systems, where it received the Best Demo Award.  To facilitate understanding and utilization, a detailed tutorial on setting up and utilizing DistQualityEvaluation has been made available.  This pioneering work lays the foundation for further research into the development of efficient, distributed methods for evaluating the consistency of RDF datasets. This study presents spatially resolved ion emission and absorption within a Seyfert5 galaxy, adding to a rare class of objects that include narrow-line tails and ionized large-scale plumes in galaxies with active nuclear regions. We label these features "ionized startled tails." Through spectral line modeling, we find ionized startled tails exhibit high ionization levels and gas velocities of approximately 1000 km/s, significantly greater than the velocities seen in broader ionized gas. We also discover a large ionization gradient along 20 kpc of one such tail, along with a critical angle of approximately 45 degrees, where the ionization drops substantially. This phenomenon persists despite line emission maps indicating a gas stream or shell at this angle. Our research further identifies a pair of broad cold absorption systems connected to a small-scale ionized structure and a much larger ionized startled tail. These systems have different velocities and are separated by approximately 10,000 km/s. They also exhibit distinct ionization levels, with the smaller structure showing higher ionization than the larger tail, which is consistent with a scenario where the gas in the smaller structure is moving towards the active nuclear region and the gas in the larger structure is moving away. This velocity separation is consistent with the velocity gradient along the axis of the active nuclear region. Our study provides strong evidence that a massive gas stream with high ionization levels can produce absorption that is caused by the gas being ionized on the front side and absorbed on the back side, resulting in a phenomenon of startled ionization wherever this stream is bent around the curve of the active nuclear region. This discovery has significant implications for interpreting the ionized gas and absorption within active galaxies, highlighting the importance of three-dimensional maps of ion emission and absorption, which can reveal the direction of gas streams and velocities, as well as identify ionized startled tails. This, in turn, affects our understanding of gas streams and outflows in active galaxies and the potential impact of these features on the surrounding intergalactic medium. It also raises the possibility that the ionized startled tails discovered in galaxy mergers may be a common phenomenon, created by the collision of gas streams during galaxy interactions. A combined ergodicity in sequences occurs when the ergodicity of one sequence is enhanced due to the action of another sequence, despite the individual sequences not exhibiting ergodic behavior. This concept is introduced through the ergodic multiplier function, which measures the combined ergodicity of two sequences, and is characterized via the distribution function of partial sums and system view. Furthermore, combined ergodicity is shown to imply the ergodicity of combined sequences, and conditions are provided for when this implication holds. Additionally, we explore the ergodicity of sequences based on lacunary series and trigonometric series, and demonstrate that combined ergodicity can arise in sequences of integers, although it requires the presence of absolutely convergent series. This work expands on previous research by D. J. H. Smeets and M. T. Lakin on combined ergodicity.

Low-resolution models were used to create initial conditions for higher-resolution models of collapsing molecular clouds, which resulted in large superbubble boundaries (up to 19 parsecs in diameter) and expanding shell walls at approximately 42 kilometers per second. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray transient IGR J19294+1816 during its 2019 outburst. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the presence of a low-frequency Quasi Periodic Oscillation and a cyclotron absorption line, with energies below their pre-eclipse levels, indicating a significant change in the line's energy due to a change in the line's orientation over a short period. This, coupled with the decrease in the orbital phase resolution, can be attributed to the binary orbit being fully covered by the accretion disk during the eclipse. A fit of the spectral data under this scenario confirmed the mass of the compact object to be less than 1.44 Solar masses, consistent with the presence of a Type a binary. Additionally, the detection of the cyclotron line at a relatively low energy supports the idea of an inner disk being present in this system. Further research using global network observations and a more in-depth analysis of the data is recommended.

The development of advanced sensing technologies for the detection of air velocity patterns is crucial in improving safety at power plants, reducing the risk of electrical discharges, and preventing the accumulation of hot gases in electrical substations. We present a cost-effective, two-dimensional laser Doppler velocimetry system that utilizes a single-point measurement system and is operated remotely. This system offers a more practical solution for real-time gas-turbine engine monitoring. We examine the technical challenges associated with scaling up the system to measure two-dimensional velocities and present a method for calculating average velocities through proper spatial sampling. We validate our system by comparing its measurements with those obtained using a reference 2D LDV system and find that it effectively detects distortions in airflow patterns. We also investigate the effect of increasing the distance between the measurement point and the mirror on the accuracy of the system, demonstrating that it is possible to achieve accurate measurements at distances of up to 20 meters. We conclude that a single-point 2D LDV system has significant applications in the monitoring of gas-turbine engines and other industrial processes that involve the transportation of hot gases across various velocities. We make available the design parameters of our 2D LDV system, encouraging its adoption by professionals in the field of power generation. We suggest potential areas for the system's further development, including the integration of temperature measurements and the detection of airflow patterns in directions perpendicular to the mirror axis. We invite researchers to explore these opportunities and contribute to the advancement of gas-turbine engine monitoring technology. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Additionally, we determine the temperature at which the thermal capacity transitions to a quadratic temperature dependence, finding it to be a function of the doping level and velocity of charge carriers. We verify our results using numerical simulations and demonstrate that the finite-temperature corrections to the thermal capacity can be significant, with the ratio of the thermal capacity to the Fermi-liquid-like portion displaying a non-intuitive, highly anisotropic doping dependence. This anisotropic doping dependence arises due to the distinct doping dependencies of the velocity of charge carriers and the density of states, with implications for the design of graphene-based materials with optimized thermal properties.  High doping levels, however, lead to a different failure mode, characterized by a sharp drop in the thermal capacity and compressibility resulting from the doping of the Dirac cones. The development of advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques for speech generation has accelerated in recent years. Despite significant progress, existing systems lack the ability to effectively consider context, a feature that is fundamental to both human language and speech. To address this limitation, we introduce MaskedSpeech, a novel context-aware speech production model that builds upon BERT-like architectures. By incorporating masking strategies, MaskedSpeech enhances the integration of contextual information, enabling the generation of more natural and coherent speech. Experimental evaluations reveal that this approach yields substantial improvements in speech quality and overall coherency. Notably, MaskedSpeech achieves notable gains in speech generation tasks, surpassing state-of-the-art baseline models like Transformer and Child-BERT, with gains of +0.56 in mean opinion score. Furthermore, MaskedSpeech exhibits adaptability in multi-task settings, demonstrating a key advantage over its non-MaskedSpeech counterpart. We also explore the effect of varying masking strategies and find that simple baseline strategies already yield satisfactory performance, indicating that these models are relatively robust. To facilitate replication and advancement, we make available the source code, pre-trained models, and datasets used in our studies. With the introduction of MaskedSpeech, we lay the groundwork for exploring context in speech production, an area that holds significant potential for future research and innovation. Two key research directions merit particular attention: the integration of paragraph-level context and the development of speech models that can learn from feedback. We anticipate that the evaluation frameworks and data sets established in this work will prove useful in investigating these issues further. In the realm of speech, the consideration of context poses an intriguing question: does context aid the generation of natural-sounding speech? reveals that a diffusive model capturing the dynamics of IKNM can be employed to model cell fate decision-making. A

and the spatial organization of nuclei during this phase. Our study demonstrates that by combining high-resolution,
high-speed three-dimensional imaging of living tissues, we can achieve a deeper understanding of the underlying
mechanisms responsible for generating the patterns that govern cell behavior and ultimately, cell fate. A related video is

Instagram has evolved into a vital platform for politicians to engage with voters, enabling them to express opinions and participate in ongoing discussions. By analyzing comments left by voters under posts made by politicians, we can gain insight into the underlying dynamics of their conversations. However, there is a lack of understanding regarding the cointeraction networks that govern these discussions. To fill this knowledge gap, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of voter comments on the accounts of Indian politicians during the 2019 Indian General Election. Utilizing a custom-made algorithm to identify relevant co-interactions, we extracted co-interaction triples from 4500 posts made by 18 politicians, resulting in a dataset comprising 157 million voters and featuring distinct temporal activity patterns. Furthermore, we observed that politicians with greater following counts tend to spark more active discussions, but struggle to sustain engagement over time. Moreover, we discovered that voters' participation exhibits seasonal fluctuations, peaking during election day and showing a clear diurnal pattern with increased activity in the evening. To further explore these findings, we developed two new measures of influence, namely, co-temporal reach and co-temporal impact, which provide a temporal perspective on a voter's ability to initiate and contribute to discussions. We found that voters exhibiting these patterns are often re-elected and tend to maintain a strong online presence. Additionally, we identified three primary topics of discussion, namely, development, corruption, and nationalism, which receive consistent attention from voters, with some voters consistently contributing to these topics and demonstrating a sense of leadership within the online community. To better explore the temporal aspects of these co-interaction networks, we conducted a dynamic network perspective analysis, which reveals that the underlying structure of these discussions evolves over time, with changes occurring every few days. We observed that some voters exhibit a sense of persistence, consistently contributing to discussions across various topics, while others prefer to focus on a single topic. Furthermore, we found that voters with a broader online presence tend to exhibit persistence more frequently. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the co-interaction networks that govern political conversations on Instagram, with implications for politicians seeking to engage with voters through online discussions. To achieve this, we offer a perspective that emphasizes the importance of persistently contributing to discussions on various topics, with a focus on building a sense of community and leadership online. This is particularly crucial during election campaigns, with voters placing a high value on politicians with a strong online presence and a history of initiating and sustaining discussions. These findings suggest that loss function variation may result in models that exhibit inductive bias, with significant implications for both theoretical and practical aspects. With the loss function being a critical component of model architecture, we propose the concept of relative classification risk to quantify the impact of loss function variation. This metric serves as a model-agnostic indicator of loss function's effect on classification performance. We also introduce an algorithmic framework that leverages this risk metric to recommend loss function alternatives for underperforming models. This approach involves generating a diverse range of loss function samples through evolutionary algorithms, with the resulting models then being used to create an ensemble of classifiers. This research provides a foundation for exploring the impact of loss function variation in deep learning through the lens of classification, offering a suite of practical solutions for enhancing classification performance. With the ever-expanding use cases for deep learning in classification, understanding the effects of loss function variation is essential, and our research opens up new avenues for theoretical exploration. Furthermore, our proposals for mitigating the negative effects of loss function variation, such as performance degradation and bias amplification during training, position deep learning in classification on a more stable foundation. With the continuous advancements in deep learning leading to improved representation capabilities, our results suggest that these advancements may, in part, be attributed to the complex interaction between loss function variation and the inherent properties of classification. This research further establishes the significance of distinct loss function relations and reveals that diverse loss functions can result in highly divergent performance metrics, even with optimal model hyperparameters. With the widespread adoption of deep learning in disciplines that rely heavily on classification, our research has significant implications, highlighting the importance of carefully selecting loss functions that account for the inherent characteristics of classification. This necessity is particularly pronounced when deploying machine learning in domains with low data points, as even slight performance deviations can significantly impact real-world applications. We introduce an innovative method, visually aided cluster ranking, that leverages human feedback to identify distinct groups within a trajectory dataset by providing ratings on their overall coherence. With the assumption that trajectories within the same cluster share a common reward, we demonstrate that human input for cluster identification is sufficiently informative to determine the underlying clustering structure and thus the individual rewards. Through experimentation, our visually aided cluster ranking approach is shown to be an efficient means of obtaining this information, and we find that using deep learning represents a viable means of transferring the learned rewards to new environments. Notably, our approach yields comparable performance to existing reward learning methods while requiring an order of magnitude less human labeling. A fundamental issue in the foundations of mathematics is the Continuum problem, which seeks to establish the cardinality of the continuum $|\mathbb{R}|$. This problem is a key milestone in solving the problems listed by Hilbert in his 1900 address. Although it has been over a century since its proposal, the Continuum problem remains an open question and one of the most significant unsolved problems in mathematics. Recently, model-theoretic concepts such as the independence of the theory of pairs of models have gained prominence as potential approaches to addressing this problem. This article aims to introduce these more elaborate methods of independence within the broader context of model theory and then apply them to a simplified scenario involving pairs of models. We demonstrate that when the independence of these pairs is established under certain conditions, it has implications for the cardinality of the continuum. Specifically, we show that if we have two models, one representing the natural numbers and the other representing the real numbers, and assuming that neither model can be covered by a subset of the other model, we can deduce that the real numbers have a cardinality greater than the natural numbers. This conclusion holds without the need for additional axioms. However, it should be noted that the most complex instances of these models can cover each other, which means that this approach cannot yield a unique solution to the Continuum problem. It is possible to formulate axioms that would lead to $|\mathbb{R}| = |\mathbb{N}|$, or alternatively, $|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{\mathbb{N}}$. Nonetheless, this article presents an unaxiomatized solution to the Continuum problem by providing an independent proof of the real numbers having a cardinality greater than the natural numbers. It is worth mentioning that this article's content has already been partially addressed in informal discussions with Silvanus, although those conversations predated his formal publication of his findings. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The complex interplay of quantum tunneling, Coulomb blockage, and Josephson junctions is complex and demands further investigation to fully clarify the underlying mechanisms in these devices. The technological potential of gate-controlled superconducting nanowires suggests the need for a deeper understanding of these phenomena, especially in relation to the development of quantum sensors and the demonstration of quantum computation. The challenge remains to construct working devices on the basis of coherent quantum phase slips while achieving the necessary level of quantum coherence over sufficient periods. This analysis also uncovers evidence of molecular layers in GJ 229B's atmosphere that differ from previously reported content, resulting in a more detailed picture of this object that improves our understanding of the few known objects of its type. Additionally, this study highlights the capabilities of the APOLLO code in analyzing distant celestial objects utilizing limited, existing data, thereby providing a valuable perspective on its potential applications.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by several interplaying factors, including the position of individuals, respiratory particle dispersal, and temperature and humidity levels. To better understand and quantify this complex phenomenon, we've found that using a well-mixed model for predicting disease transmission is inaccurate. In our study, we've put forth a robust approach that utilizes a numerical model for simulating air particle dispersal. Our findings show that using this approach for two specific scenarios results in predictions that are more accurate than a well-mixed framework. Our approach also suggests that using models that account for respiratory particle dispersal could reduce the estimated transmission risk by as much as 99%. We believe our study provides valuable insights that can be applied to a broader range of enclosed environments beyond urban buses. It suggests that using a well-mixed framework for modeling disease transmission in urban buses may lead to an overestimation of 10 to 1000 times. We've made our data and analysis publicly available to inform control strategies and the design of bus interiors to reduce the transmission risk. We recommend exploring this approach further to develop effective strategies to control the transmission of airborne pathogens in confined environments. In quantum key distribution, a crucial process called measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) is considered the most secure way to generate secret keys, leveraging the quantum principle of linear channel attenuation to detect malicious behavior of the communication network. However, there is a significant limitation to implementing MDI-QKD over extended distances - it requires the use of entangled resource, which drastically reduces the length of generated keys. To overcome this hurdle, researchers have proposed converting classical key generation into a quantum process called quantum backwards reconciliation, utilizing classical source coding and involving all parties in the communication network. Notably, this conversion enables the use of classical reconciliation instead of quantum state merging, the original process used in QKD. As such, it allows key generation in noisy channels without the need for entangled resources. Although this modification allows key generation in noisy channels, it introduces the risk of malicious behavior by network participants. To detect such tampering, researchers have proposed incorporating an additively white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel and developed a novel demonstration of the security of this modified process. The proposed demonstration relies on the unique characteristics of Gaussian distributions to distinguish malicious behavior and maintains the same success rate in demonstrating the security of MDI-QKD, even when the amount of noise in the communication network is increased. Furthermore, this demonstration reduces the accuracy of channel estimation but still successfully identify the attack in up to 95% of cases. Notably, this reduction in accuracy does not result in the duplication of the shared secret, as it occurs rarely enough. Nonetheless, this proposal may be vulnerable to a novel attack that allows the detection of the measurement basis attack in exchange for a small decrease in the density of noise in the communication network. Although this attack is detectable in the demonstration, it still presents an interesting consideration for extending the length of generated keys in MDI-QKD over extended distances. To address this issue, researchers may consider implementing a novel modulation scheme that converts the measurement device independent encoding used in MDI-QKD into a key generation process that is secure against malicious behavior by network participants, allowing the use of entangled resources without reducing the length of generated keys. This novel modulation scheme maintains the same success rate in demonstrating the security of MDI-QKD when the amount of noise in the communication network is increased and reduces the required noise in the Gaussian distribution by up to 50%. Furthermore, it increases the ratio of information carrying capacity to the required entangled resources in up to 95% of cases, significantly enhancing the potential of MDI-QKD

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to the input data they are predicting, without considering real-world challenges such as varying scanner types, different radiopharmaceuticals, and diverse patient populations, which significantly impact the performance of these models. This research introduces a novel uncertainty-aware neural network framework that incorporates physics-based transformations and adapts to unexpected PET-MRI combinations it encounters during inference, allowing for the generation of high-quality PET images at lower doses. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of this method through imaging systems and tissues it had never seen before during both simulated and actual experiments. Notably, our method outperformed existing models in enhancing PET images from lower doses, even without using additional training data. Additionally, our results indicate that this technique can generate high-quality PET images at half the usual dose without the need for additional training, surpassing state-of-the-art deep learning models that only performed better on in-distribution tests. This uncertainty-aware framework can facilitate the creation of low-dose PET images in clinical settings with various PET-MRI data, even if such combinations were not included in the training data. This model has the potential to enhance real-world PET images, especially in areas with limited access to high-dose PET scanners. We have open-sourced our model and source code on GitHub, and it has been incorporated into the Toulouse Deep Learning Platform for Medical Image Analysis (TDL-PMA). We have also submitted an accompanying technical report to the 2022 Medical Image Analysis Workshop on Deep Learning the Liver (LIVER-2022). This study has been funded in part by ANR-ADGA Grant No. ANR-20-CHIL-0008 and the University of Toulouse. All experiments were conducted on Tesla V100 20GB GPUs. We have already integrated this research into an upcoming paper accepted at the 2023 Medical Image Analysis Conference. We have obtained the required ethics approvals for conducting low-dose PET enhancements on actual patients at the University Hospitals of Toulouse. We have established a publicly accessible low-dose PET enhancement challenge on Codalab, available at https://codalab.org/

Adapting online services and products to individual needs is the focus of personalized technology. However, it raises significant concerns about the compromise of privacy and difficulty of control over personalized settings. To better understand these issues, a survey of 4,197 adults in the United States was conducted, yielding notable findings: nearly 9 in 10 participants felt that reducing privacy was an acceptable price for personalized experiences, but this sentiment dropped to below 25% when the potential loss of employment or social rejection was factored in; the majority of participants desired more control over data collection and the ability to opt out of unnecessary customization; and there was a noticeable discrepancy between the willingness of younger and older adults to pay for private, non-personalized services, with the former showing little inclination and the latter showing a strong inclination. These findings have implications for companies that offer personalized services and products, suggest that there is a noticeable difference in the behaviors of younger and older adults, and highlight the importance of giving users more control over data collection and the ability to customize settings that cater to their privacy concerns. To address these issues, we propose an interactive system that allows users to balance privacy and functionality by prioritizing individual needs and adapting to user input via a user-friendly interface, providing a model that incorporates privacy considerations in decision-making processes, and offering custom-built models that can be applied to various domains and platforms. By speeding up the customization process and providing transparent information, this system aims to make personalized technology more appealing to users who value privacy. Experimental results show that this system produces high-quality solutions that are comparable to those generated by expert users, is user-friendly and easy to use, and performs well in complex scenarios. It has the potential to be applied to various domains and platforms, such as recommendation systems, machine learning, and data mining applications.
