A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper investigates the link between CT and modern computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study finds that a computer system's ability to recognize these connections is related to the coherence of the text. However, this coherence is not solely dependent on the accuracy of the coreference resolution, suggesting that there are other factors at play. The study also demonstrates that there is variability in how different computer systems that are trained on the same data, but have the same performance in identifying these connections, judge the importance of statements. This phenomenon is particularly evident when the statements are not directly about the main topic, and it is further amplified in more complex texts. The study's findings imply that these computer systems do not necessarily capture the underlying principles of CT, and it is not clear whether they are just emulating the training data or truly understanding the connections between statements. As a result, they may not be the best tools to evaluate the CT's predictions about the coherence of conversations. The study recommends that more rigorous testing is needed to validate the predictions made by CT in relation to the coherence of conversations, and it suggests that there may be benefits in re-examining the assumptions made when designing the computer systems that identify relationships within a text. The study's findings are relevant to both the fields of natural language processing and linguistics. The paper discusses the computer systems that were used in the experiments and makes available the code that was developed for the project's evaluations. The study's findings are also relevant to the issue of making predictions with multiple possible answers, and it is hoped that they will inspire a re-evaluation of the computer systems that are used in other tasks that involve this type of prediction. The study is a theoretical examination of the link between CT and the computer systems that identify relationships within a text, and it is hoped that a more practical experiment will be conducted in the future to test some of the study's claims. The study is relevant to both the University of Pennsylvania and the New University of Lisbon. The study is a demonstration of how the knowledge of experienced linguists can be combined with the knowledge of computer systems to gain a deeper understanding of the connections between statements, and it is hoped that it will inspire a more collaborative approach between these two fields. In 1960, Freeman Dyson proposed using extensive networks of light sails to capture a significant portion of the energy emitted by a distant star. This concept could potentially support an infinite number of advanced civilizations by providing necessary energy while minimizing visible signs of the civilization. A similar idea, introduced in this paper, suggests constructing a massive structure in the form of a shell around a black hole to capture its surrounding energy. However, due to the extreme gravitational forces at play, any object drawing close to the shell would be pulled apart by tidal forces, imposing significant constraints on the shell's design. This paper presents a novel configuration, dubbed the "Rosenberg Shell," that meets these environmental demands. The shell's effectiveness in capturing energy is maximized when its edges are just 7.5 million kilometers from the event horizon, allowing it to capture nearly 30% of the energy emitted by a star while providing about 10% of the energy to a civilization located close to the shell. This paper also explores different variations of this concept, including one where the shell is used to split energy between two civilizations sitting on opposite sides of the black hole. This configuration, however, due to the shell's narrow effective capture range, is limited to stars no more than 2.5 kiloparsecs away. A more substantial increase in the shell's size, to a diameter of about 100 astronomical units, could potentially capture a larger star up to 2.5 kiloparsecs in distance, but it would make the structure visible from Earth. This idea may offer a basis for developing a protocol to detect Dyson Shells around stars over time. A software package called GAbel, publicly available and easily accessible through a web interface, allows users to generate variations of the Rosenberg Shell and identify similar structures surrounding stars. This package utilizes data from the Kepler K2 mission and a filter applied to the data that indicates the presence of a variable signal affecting about 10% of the stars monitored. No evidence of the Rosenberg Shell or similar structures surrounding these stars could be found. This discovery doesn't rule out the existence of these shells, but it indicates they are extremely rare or are constructed for a different purpose, such as marking a civilization's location or serving a functional purpose. Lastly, this paper suggests that constructing a Dyson Shell around a white dwarf or a neutron star may be feasible with present-day energy output, offering a marker 98% certain of its presence and capable of being detected by telescopes capable of analyzing the star's surrounding environment. The beam breakup instability in an energy recovery linac has significant implications for efficient power recovery and it is crucial to assess its impact through detailed design considerations. This paper delves into the design of the filling pattern and its influence on the beam breakup instability, revealing how certain filling patterns can reduce the electric field threshold and minimize the energy spread, ultimately facilitating lower charge beam operation and increased power recovery potential. Various filling patterns are discussed, including their effects on beam dynamics and electromagnetic field development. We also examine the criteria for beam and electromagnetic field alignment, discussing the advantages of certain filling patterns over others. Experimental validation is performed at the DESERVE test stand using a 1.5 GeV, single-bunch electron beam, and the results demonstrate the dependence of beam breakup instability and energy spread on filling pattern, aligning with numerical simulations, and demonstrating the feasibility of applying this technology at the 3 GeV scale. Introduction  Beam breakup instability (BBU) caused by the interaction between a charged particle beam and the electromagnetic field it generates has significant implications for the efficient operation of an energy recovery linac (ERL). It represents a design constraint that typically limits the beam charge and, consequently, the power that can be recovered from an ERL. For this reason, understanding the factors influencing BBU and developing strategies to manage its effects is crucial to realizing the full potential of ERLs in various applications, including particle acceleration, beam warfare systems, and x-ray and free-electron lasers. For example, in particle acceleration applications, BBU usually limits the achievable beam charge and, consequently, the number of particles that can be accelerated in a given period, leading to increased energy recovery time and, ultimately, reduced efficiency in power recovery. In this paper, we examine the factors that influence BBU in an ERL and discuss ways to manage its effects by manipulating the filling pattern, beam energy spread, and electric field threshold. We present experimental data obtained with a filling pattern that reduces the energy spread and electric field threshold, confirming that it results in lower charge beam operation and increased power recovery potential. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the design of ERLs at the 3 GeV scale. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all kinematic configurations. The derived two-gluon CEV exhibits significant imaginary components across its support and varying signs, contrasting initial predictions. Its behavior is influenced by several poles, including an additional one at $\chi=0$, contributing to a discontinuity in the real part as a function of the rapidity gap. Additionally, modifications to the CEV to account for processes like quark and ghost emissions have been proposed, though these are subject to confirmation by further explicit calculations. The results obtained are in line with expectations based on systematics of N=4 SYM theory at small and medium rapidity gap configurations. A numerical assessment of the real and imaginary components of the two-gluon CEV is provided, revealing how they transform under changes in the rapidity gap and central-emission rapidity, including an interesting flip in the sign of the imaginary part as the latter exceeds a certain threshold. The intricate relationship between knotted protein structures and their functional availability within the cellular environment remains somewhat unclear. Recent research suggests that the presence of knots in proteins is more common than previously thought, with approximately twenty-five percent of naturally occurring proteins exhibiting some level of knotting. It has also been proposed that the space of knotted protein structures is divided into distinct regions, each corresponding to a unique knot type, referred to as a "knot seed". Notwithstanding these advancements, the process by which proteins become knotted and the reason why this phenomenon is so prevalent across nature remain to be fully comprehended. This study introduces the concept of using knotted protein structures in conjunction with advanced mathematical topological tools to predict and visualize the pathways available for bond breaking and reformation. Our research reveals that these predicted pathways differ significantly for proteins with trefoil knots as compared to proteins with their analogues in higher-order knots, specifically with regards to the cross-over number. Moreover, we find that the trefoil knot proteins exhibit a more confined distribution compared to their counterparts in higher-order knots when considering the space of native states. Furthermore, our results indicate that the available space of low-energy states for trefoil knot proteins is separated into two distinct components, each corresponding to a unique set of bending pathways. This distinction enables us to create a classification system for proteins based on their knot types and protein sequences, and to explore the relationship between protein structure and function through the lens of topology. Our research paves the way for a novel approach that integrates experimental and computational studies of knotted proteins, and may yield valuable insights for the broader field of protein folding. This integrated perspective may also offer a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between protein structure, the cellular environment, and protein function, and could provide a useful framework for the development of future proteomics technologies. Early Dark Energy (EDE) has gained significant attention as a promising explanation for resolving the Hubble tension. EDE models typically introduce a significant cosmological constant at very early times, which leads to a distinctive signal in the small-scale power spectrum. To accurately place constraints on these models, it's essential to consider the impact of Gaussian fluctuations on the power spectrum. By accounting for these fluctuations, the 95% confidence interval for the logarithm of the EDE amplitude shifts from approximately 0.07 to 0.10, with a slight decrease in the mean due to mild bias. Under this revised framework, the EDE solution to the Hubble tension is slightly reduced, with the 95% confidence interval now ranging from 0.03 to 0.08. When combining Planck and BOSS data using the standard profile likelihood method, the constraint on the EDE amplitude becomes more stringent, with an upper limit of 0.05. However, when applying the corrected analysis, this limit increases to 0.07, with models having 0.04 < log10(1+ΔEDE) < 0.09 in 1σ confidence. Conversely, the best-fit model with no spatial variations in the neutrino mass moves the start of EDE from the Big Bang to within 0.03 comoving gigaparsecs (Gpc-1) from the present time, with a corresponding increase in the effective number of neutrinos(Neff) to around 3.18, resulting in a slight decrease in the χ2 by 5.3 for the Planck+BOSS data combination. Nonetheless, the constraint on the start of EDE remains loose enough to support the possibility of the EDE amplitude increasing with increasing scale, as indicated by recent observations, without significant conflict. We provide a comprehensive explanation of a recent finding related to symplectic mapping classes on the blowups of four-dimensional symplectic tori. It was established by Huang-Li's research that the space of these mappings possesses a structure analogous to category for a certain range of symplectic capacities. We expand upon their results by showing that this relationship holds without limitations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in the context of a particular set of symplectic capacities, where the capacity of a point is equal to the sum of the capacities of the components after blowing up, there are mappings that increase the category by two while keeping the capacity of the point at one. This achievement relies on the development of a novel family of symplectic embeddings on the blowup of a torus in four-dimensional space. These embeddings establish a connection between the category of the blowup and a certain pattern formed by Legendrian curves. It was previously unknown whether such a relationship like this one could be achieved through symplectic mappings alone. Moreover, our research introduces a new method for creating symplectic mappings on the blowup of a four-dimensional torus by identifying a type of area where embeddings can occur more easily. This method may be applicable to higher-dimensional space. Additionally, we demonstrate that there are mappings that expand the category of the blowup by three while keeping the capacity of the point at two. These achievements are crucial for proving that the space of symplectic mapping classes on the blowup of a four-dimensional symplectic torus is infinite in cardinality for a certain range of symplectic capacities. It was a long-standing question whether the space of symplectic mapping classes on the blowup of a four-dimensional symplectic torus could be finite in cardinality. It was first proposed by Guttreich in 1990 and later proposed again by Halwachs in 2006. It is worth noting that Polterovich-Sikorav's work in 2000 provided a mapping that increased the category by two while keeping the capacity of the point at one in the context of a particular set of symplectic capacities. However, their work was done before the space of symplectic mapping classes on the blowup of a four-dimensional symplectic torus was well-defined. A detailed investigation of the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) boson phenomenon is conducted through a general analysis of the symmetry breaking and NG theorem in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories. The study emphasizes the importance of a unitary and symmetry-breaking pattern in order to yield nontrivial NG bosons. In contrast, bosonic symmetry and unitarity lead to flat potential surfaces, resulting in zero mass NG bosons. The evaluation of the NG boson mass matrix relies on the representation of nonrelativistic NG bosons as bound states of nonrelativistic particle-antiparticle pairs, allowing for the interpretation of the NG theorem within the framework of nonrelativistic quantum mechanics and field theory. A comparison between the contributions of internal and external symmetries in relation to NG bosons is also presented, revealing that only internal symmetries lead to the existence of NG bosons, as exemplified through the Sp(2N) symmetric matrix models of fermion-fermion and boson-boson condensation. A key finding of this research is the proposal of theories involving multiple NG bosons and the prediction of the mass spectra of these theories. A unitary Sp(2N+2) symmetry is applied to a fermionic matrix model, resulting in (N-1) masses of the NG bosons and a single massive state, while a unitary Sp(4N) symmetry yields N distinct mass scales with nonrelativistic power-law behaviors. These theories can be experimentally verified through the measurement of NG boson mass spectra in the regulation of symmetry-breaking phases and the characterization of the low-energy effective theories. A further exploration of the relationship between the Sp(2N) symmetry and the Higgs boson is also discussed. A similar power-law behavior is observed in a bosonic matrix model with a unitary U(2N) symmetry, where the presence of a unitary symmetry leads to the formation of a condensate that gives mass to all fermion species within the same representation. A further extension to a unitary U(2N+2) symmetry results in (N-1) masses of the NG bosons and a single massive state in both the Sp(2N) and U(2N) cases, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the unusual NG theorem. Reasoning about combinations of entities and their hypothetical attributes is a fundamental skill that's not well developed in current language models. This task is critical in understanding how language models handle complex, multi-faceted statements and situations. Such an ability would also permit more effective improvement of language models through training on real-world language data fortified with carefully crafted hypothetical phrases. To facilitate this process, we've created a distinct evaluation metric and a dataset consisting of phrasal hypotheticals, which we utilize to introduce a novel approach called Disco. This approach involves employing a reverse engineering method to accurately infer the intended meaning of a phrasal hypothetical by comparing the generated text to actual language produced by the same entities. The approach is a straightforward yet effective way to enhance the capacity of language models to reason about entity attributes through a process called cross-distribution distillation. When applied to large language models, this method yields remarkable performance improvements, as evidenced by significant gains in accuracy resulting from a simple model refinement technique called back-and-forth reasoning. Furthermore, our research uncovering the underlying factors that influence the ability of language models to reason about entity attributes and their attributes may also contribute valuable insights to the broader field of reasoning in natural language. To facilitate further exploration, we've made both the evaluation metric and the dataset publicly available. When evaluated against these standards, current state-of-the-art models fail to achieve above-chance performance in understanding phrasal hypotheticals. This shortfall presents an opportunity for model developers to compete in an open competition focused on improving Disco models. As part of this effort, we've established a leading baseline by developing a simple model called Hyperico that outperforms all existing models by a substantial margin. This leader has achieved an impressive 73% accuracy in evaluating the truth of phrasal hypotheticals. Although there are some instances where the model's judgment diverges from the anticipated outcome, it still offers valuable guidance to those working to enhance the ability of language models to reason about entity attributes and their attributes. To that end, we've opened up the evaluation to a wide range of models participating in yet another competition focused on this critical aspect of natural language understanding. The findings are based on the graph theorem and the sum distinguishing theorem. We found that a graph G has a neighborhood sum distinguishing chromatic number of at most k if and only if the largest component of G contains a vertex with a neighborhood sum value of less than k. We also established that a graph G has an equitable total chromatic number of at most k if and only if the largest component of G contains a vertex with a total sum value of less than k*|V(G)|. These results contribute to our knowledge of the total, equitable total, and neighborhood sum distinguishing chromatic numbers of circulant graphs on 3-cycles. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, successful remote epitaxy can only be achieved with specific film/substrate combinations, such as CoPt on habitually clean graphite surfaces, yet others like Heusler films have proven challenging. Our studies reveal that incorporating oxygen during the heating period before film deposition, rather than pre-cleaning the substrate, results in the growth of the Heusler film L2-FeGa3 through a mix of remote and van der Waals epitaxy, leading to an assortment of crystal structures and magnetic properties. Furthermore, this discovery opens up the possibility of utilizing this approach to actively select the epitaxial mode simply by adjusting the substrate temperature. Additionally, we find that introducing oxygen allows for the growth of the L2-FeGa3 phase at substantially lower temperatures, compared to its bulk form, and this effect is attributed to the formation of an oxygen layer that facilitates bond formation between the film and the substrate. This breakthrough could make it feasible to actively manage the equilibrium between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy, thereby enabling a greater variety of material properties and, as a result, a broader range of applications. This finding is particularly significant for magnetic Heusler films that typically require precise composition and structure to exhibit desired magnetic properties. This discovery could also make it possible to grow a diverse range of materials that are difficult to produce through other methods, thus giving this approach a significant advantage over conventional synthesis methods. The success of advanced machine learning models relies heavily on high-quality labeled data, but the process of manual annotation is resource-intensive and usually focused on specific key characteristics. Despite having access to detailed annotations for individual examples, it's common for only one label to be highlighted at a time, leaving numerous unexploited annotations for other features. To leverage this wealth of unlabelled information, we develop a novel multi-label sampling approach, where we utilize one positive label to generate diverse combinations of features. To achieve this, we first gather pairs of related labels for every positive example and use these connections to create a co-occurrence graph. We then craft a diverse set of candidate features for each example by extracting the most varied labels from the features that co-occur with it in the graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the process of data preparation for exponential histogram features in real-world image classification projects. We compare our method to established diversity preservation techniques and show that it results in more diverse, denser regions of the feature space, leading to better performance without the need for additional expert time. We also release an open-source Python implementation of our approach. This study proposes a new method for allocating portfolios across a given set of assets, utilizing expected returns that are cross-sectionally consistent.  By assuming that each asset's return follows a factor model, we formulate a strategy for selecting portfolios that are optimized for their returns while minimizing their risks.  However, this approach is complex to execute analytically due to the presence of constraints that are driven by the number of assets.  To overcome this difficulty, we reframe the problem so it becomes equivalent to a series of linear programs, each corresponding to a specific portfolio.  This strategy is theoretically shown to be superior to the traditional approach and is then applied to actual data, resulting in the discovery of negative aspects of diversification and the existence of skills in certain assets. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate diagnosis from cardiac auscultation sounds is challenging due to varying recording environments and the use of different microphones.  Existing research primarily focused on noise reduction, but neglected the impact of distortion.  This research analyzes both noise and distortion effects, using a combined measure of signal-to-noise and signal-to-distortion ratios.  To account for these distortions, heart sounds are represented in a new way, based on entropy measurements.  This approach enhances the accuracy of heart condition classification, with results showing an overall accuracy of 88.24%, outperforming existing methods.  The proposed technique's effectiveness is further verified through a comparison with a more advanced network, confirming its potential for clinical applications.  With an accuracy of 92.50% achieved through a larger dataset, there is scope for further improvement.  The technique's potential for detecting conditions like mitral stenosis is also explored, with future directions identified for the research.  A publicly available dataset comprising 50 recordings of 4 seconds each is made available for further heart condition research.  The simple yet effective approach based on entropy representations may inspire applications in sound classification across other areas.  All code and data utilized in the research are openly disseminated. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models for each individual user suffer from a lack of transferable knowledge from similar cases. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering framework for federated learning that enables the transfer of knowledge within wearable healthcare contexts. FedHealth comprises three key modules: FedLearner, a base learning module that facilitates model training and synchronization; FedSender, a sender module that manages data dissemination and model updates; and FedPermit, a permit module that supervises collaboration protocol and ensures security. This paper provides an in-depth examination of each component as well as the advantages of this novel approach. Experimental findings using the MIMIC-III CSV dataset demonstrate that FedHealth delivers superior performance compared to both non-transfer and single-data-case baseline models. Furthermore, the framework exhibits adaptable performance when collaborating with disparate datasets containing similar and dissimilar data cases. It also proves that FedHealth is an efficient solution with minimal communication requirements. The code for FedHealth has been made publicly accessible on GitHub. This framework is particularly relevant to addressing the ongoing pandemic pandemic by developing secure and collaborative health monitoring systems. This study tackles a control problem where costs change over time and are broken into pieces, and we aim to analyze the optimal strategy for a dynamic system that can be switched on and off, represented by a system of stochastic differential equations, subject to these varying costs. We look for a way to express the best control action in terms of the system's current state and the evolving costs, and establish some conditions under which this relationship becomes transparent. Additionally, we identify the optimal policy for a specific cost evolution, and explore the impact of a sudden change in costs on the system. Some numerical methods are also introduced to compute approximate solutions and illustrate the method's effectiveness. This research is relevant to managing systems with components that have interconnections that can be activated or deactivated. We use the LQG switching control problem as a key example, and our results are motivated by studies on a class of systems with interconnections that can be activated or deactivated, presented in the paper 'Interconnection of systems with relays' by M. Hairer, A. Neufeld, and G. Turan. Highly variable single-cell biological signal readings can benefit from advanced techniques such as multi-task learning and temporal sequence modeling to provide more accurate cell population estimates. However, due to the high dimensionality of single-cell data, traditional machine learning approaches often struggle with over-fitting and the resulting models can be difficult to interpret. To address these challenges, we propose an innovative model that leverages low-rank techniques to efficiently process high-dimensional temporal sequence data. This model utilizes guided learning to integrate multiple tasks, like single-cell RNA and gene expression data, and includes a dimensionality reduction element that simplifies the interpretation of its results. Through comprehensive simulations and real-world applications, our guided learning approach demonstrates its superiority over existing methods, like multi-task learning and matrix factorization, in producing more accurate cell population estimates and identifying key differentiating cells. Moreover, this approach outperforms the state-of-the-art in analyzing T-cell receptor sequencing data and identifies novel key genes in type 1 diabetes. Overall, our technique provides a scalable and precise way to analyze single-cell data across various applications. To facilitate the exploration of single-cell data, our algorithm also incorporates an interactive visualization tool that enables users to modify model predictions by adjusting data weightages, providing valuable insights into the underlying biology. Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition of new categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This improvement is particularly pronounced for instruments that aren't part of the training set, resulting in a significant enhancement in performance when introducing novel categories. We also test the robustness of this approach by introducing a greater number of untrained instruments in each family and find that it stands to reason that establishing a strong foundation of data for previously unidentified instruments would further enhance the results. This project is implemented using a convolutional neural network, and we observe that a hierarchical approach delivers better performance even with a simple model like this one. This research is conducted using recordings of 24 different instruments, including those that weren't sampled during the training phase, at three different dynamics (piano, mezzo-forte, and pianissimo). This encompasses 72 classes of instruments in total, representing all sections of the orchestra. To acquire a diverse dataset for testing, we gather recordings of all instruments at all dynamics from two sources: the ISMRDB and YouTube. This multi-dynamic setting delivers a greater challenge than practicing music at a moderate pace because it's harder to pinpoint the sound when the music is played loudly or softly. This difficulty is compounded by the fact that musicians often change dynamics throughout a single piece, resulting in a wide dynamic range. This means that detecting instruments under these conditions demands more precision than identifying them in music played at a consistent mezzo-forte dynamic. This project achieves the highest accuracy on a diverse dataset of musical instruments, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art method by a substantial 11.8%. This superiority is demonstrated in both scenarios where the test data shares the same instrumental structure as the training data and in scenarios where the test data presents new classes of instruments. This is the first time the top performance on this challenge has been achieved. Academic researchers who read numerous research papers usually rely on citations and existing knowledge bases for answers to fundamental questions related to those papers. However, there is a significant gap in knowledge when it comes to understanding the methodology, data, or material discussed in research papers. To bridge this knowledge gap, we have launched a new web-based platform that allows users to post questions related to research papers and receive answers from experts in the field. Each question is paired with the name of the paper, author, publication, and a link to the paper itself. We have created a diverse dataset of 1,583 question-answer pairs through a comprehensive data collection process involving various approaches to obtain relevant expertise and ensure the quality of both research papers and answers provided. We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the dataset's characteristics and discovered that nearly 40% of the knowledge gaps were regarding methods, followed closely by data at around 30%. We have further experimented with state-of-the-art cross-domain retrieval models to evaluate their performance in identifying relevant information from a diverse range of research papers. Unfortunately, these powerful retrieval models struggled to strike a balance between accuracy and coherence. As a result, we propose a simple alternative approach that involves ranking answers based on their overall coherence. This approach not only simplifies the complex issue at hand but also significantly improves the effectiveness of the recommended answers. We have pre-trained our proposed approach on the newly created dataset consisting of over 1,500 question-answer pairs and found that it achieves exceptional coherence at a reasonable level of accuracy. We have also explored various ways to assess the validity of the answers provided and the associated research papers. We have launched an open-call for both expert answers and validity assessments covering a wide range of topics and have made the newly created dataset available for benchmarking various state-of-the-art cross-domain retrieval models. We have obtained impressive results with our proposed approach, a simple 8-layer transformer model known as "ResearchPaperAnswerer." We have obtained evidence that our proposed approach generalizes well across different research papers covering various topics and has significantly outperformed all the baselines we have created, including some highly-advanced cross-domain retrieval models. We have further experimented with the idea of combining our proposed approach with state-of-the-art question-answering models to evaluate their performance in identifying relevant answers from a diverse range of research papers. We have obtained mixed results, with our proposed approach performing exceptionally well on questions related to methodology but struggling with data and material-related questions. We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a velocity process emerges that converges to a random walk driven by a specific rate, and we prove that this convergence occurs at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ for systems starting with $k$ connected steps. Additionally, we find that the speed of this velocity process is independent of whether the steps in ASEP are oriented in a symmetric manner or not. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable breakthroughs in understanding three-dimensional topological insulators and has recently focused on two-dimensional Dirac materials. Consequently, the nodal line, a one-dimensional topological feature, now attracts substantial attention. This review aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the theoretical concepts underlying nodal line physics and showcase recent implementations using photonic structures, mechanical systems, and metamaterials. We contend that the nodal line, often described using a parameter (without considering magnetic field influence), is fundamentally a two-dimensional singular point in momentum space. Its realization is possible through the appropriate design of structures that incorporate a singular point in momentum space, which is not necessarily a topological feature. However, when a magnetic field is introduced, the nodal line becomes a topological concept, and its realization is demonstrated in variously designed structures that demonstrate the unique properties of topological insulators. We anticipate that the exploration of topological phenomena in mechanical, optical systems, and other contexts will provide valuable insights to benefit the broader field of condensed matter research. Additionally, the relatively loose relationships between frequency, Weyl points, and Fermi velocity velocities in these systems offer opportunities for even more complex and intricate topological phenomena. We propose that the term "Weyl point" be used to describe both four-dimensional and six-dimensional singular points in momentum space that are characterized by a cubic term in momentum and a five-dimensional singular point in momentum space that is characterized by a quadratic term, respectively. Furthermore, we suggest that the term "3D Weyl point" be used to describe a four-dimensional singular point in momentum space that is characterized by a quadratic term and that the Hall conductivity in these systems can be precisely measured using the technique of time-reversal optical photography. Lastly, we outline potential avenues for exploring topological physics in photonic and other systems through the theoretical concept of nodal line physics. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent contradiction between the network's training objectives of maximizing classification accuracy and minimizing uncertainty. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the network's training energy to model uncertainty in an open-world setting. By incorporating an auxiliary uncertainty variable that is derived from the network's training energy, we frame uncertainty as an optimization problem. This allows us to develop uncertainty models that are independent of data augmentation techniques and do not introduce additional hyperparameters. Our proposed method demonstrates superior performance in comparison to state-of-the-art techniques, as evidenced by the results of our experiments using the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. Notably, our method achieves a notable reduction in the Fisher information matrix, a known indicator of over-confidence, and significantly outperforms the baseline in terms of ECE calibration. Additionally, our method exhibits robust performance in the presence of label noise. We also explore the connection between energy minimization and the Riesz representation theorem, providing a theoretical justifications for our approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/hjdw2/EDUOpenWorld.

Parallel programs rely on synchronization primitives like locks and fences to ensure
the consistency of shared memory. However, errors in parallel programs can lead to
invalidations of memory fences, causing prolonged memory effects and making program
crashes difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel
approach, combining self-downgrade and self-invalidations to identify and repair
fence-related issues. By leveraging our technique, we develop an efficient and
effective tool, Fense, which locally modifies parallel programs using our repair
strategy to eliminate fence-related crashes and non-determinism. Fense achieves this
by modifying approximately 10% of the original code, and our experiments show that
it is capable of fixing intricate program errors with excellent performance results. 
Our repair strategy is versatile, however, we observe that programs with a high
degree of parallelism and many synchronization points pose a challenge for Fense.
To overcome this limitation, we introduce an optimized version of our approach,
which employs a more discerning repair strategy and produces code modifications
with a significantly lower overhead, resulting in a substantial improvement in our
benchmarks. With these enhancements, Fense is now capable of fixing complex
crashes in programs with high levels of parallelism and extensive synchronization. 
Our study demonstrates that parallel programs with fence-related issues often
exhibit poor performance, however, after repair, the programs run at full system speed. 
On average, Fense can fix over 90% of program crashes and non-deterministic
outcomes, and approximately 75% of the fixed programs run correctly on actual
hardware, providing a reliable method for enabling the execution of previously
crash-prone parallel programs on multi-core systems. To facilitate the use of
Fense, we have developed an intuitive user interface and incorporated various
features such as program verification, but due to space constraints, these aspects
must be explored in further research. Our approach is versatile, allowing it to
be applied to a broad range of parallel programs, and we have successfully tested
it with programs written in C11 and C++11, as well as OpenCL. Furthermore, we have
also explored the application of our repair strategy to sequential programs with
mutexes and atomic operations, and have obtained promising results with our early
stages of development indicating that our approach may also be effective for

Recent advancements in laser-guided astrobots enable efficient and scalable fiber feeders, thereby maximizing survey efficiency. To function properly, these astrobots rely on a sophisticated safe coordination system, a technology that we test and refine using a fully functional prototype in conjunction with the SDSS-V's 105 fiber feeders. Our experiments demonstrate that the system's top-performing configuration achieves a coordinate success rate of over 99.9% and is capable of coordinating all astrobots in under 20 seconds. Furthermore, we find that a zone-based partitioning system reduces the incidence of unsafe configurations by a factor of nearly 100, and that a dynamic version of this approach is capable of adapting to an astrobot failure rate of up to 20%. We also observe that a rule-based system can recover from unsafe configurations resulting from astrobot malpositioning, and that a combination of this recovery system and the dynamic zone-based system can handle astrobot failures and malpositioning alike. Additionally, we explore methods to minimize the distance astrobots need to travel and find that these strategies can reduce the time it takes to coordinate all astrobots by up to a factor of ten; however, they often result in the exclusion of a survey target. We discuss the implications of these findings for the optimization of safe coordination and present a framework for solving this problem computationally. Finally, we anticipate that the next generation of laser-guided astrobots, featuring improved laser technology and better mechanical design, will further enhance the system's performance. With the development of its prototype, the field of safe astrobot coordination has reached a significant milestone and the technology is now ready for implementation in the SDSS-V and other scalable spectroscopic surveys. To facilitate the adoption of this technology, we have created an open-source documentation of the system, along with a comprehensive code repository that includes the safe coordination algorithm and all related software components. This code has been thoroughly tested and is fully compatible with the SDSS-V's data reduction software, called PFS-RED. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently implementing GP 2 dependencies within a host language like Java or C# is complicated, as it requires meticulous consideration of reference equality, cache behavior, and side-effects. To overcome these difficulties, the GP 2 community developed a suite of compilers that can effectively translate GP 2 programs into the host language, leveraging domain-specific language principles to simplify implementation challenges. These compilers enhance the underlying host languages with necessary extensions, ensuring that GP 2 programs can be executed with optimal performance. This work explores the design of the GP 2 compilers, discussing the underlying language principles, reference equality management, cache optimization, and side-effect handling. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these compilers, a case study showcases how they can be used to develop a program analyzer, leveraging their performance benefits. The GP 2 compilers are now open-source, contributing to the GP 2 research community. The GP 2 compilers are available at https://github.com/gp2-research/gp2-compiler. The case study is described at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.00675. The GP 2 community is invited to engage with these innovations. The GP 2 compilers are an evolution of the GP 2 tools, replacing the legacy GP 3 compilers. The GP 2 compilers are backward-compatible with GP 3 programs, requiring only minor adaptations to function correctly. The GP 2 compilers can also utilize the GP 3 analyzers in their current form, thanks to the compilers' ability to detect the presence of Java 16 records and adjust their behavior accordingly. The GP 2 compilers provide two execution modes: regular execution and reflection-free execution. The regular execution mode is the default behavior, involving the creation of instance fields within objects to store dependencies. This approach facilitates fast, efficient program analysis and modification. The reflection-free execution mode is a novel feature that eliminates the use of instance fields, instead utilizing method parameters to store dependencies. This approach significantly reduces memory usage but incurs a small performance cost due to increased method invocation depth. The GP 2 compilers can translate a wide range of GP 2 programs, including those with nested rules, global variables, Java interoperation, and Java 16 records. They often employ lidar technology for scanning their environment, which produces a point cloud with significant spatial coverage. To facilitate seamless motion planning and prevent collisions, it's essential to create a movable obstacle map by combining individual point clouds from different scans. This task is equivalent to solving the panoramic joining problem, where we aim to develop an algorithm that minimizes energy expenditure and yields local maxima prior to scan merging. This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for Parkinson's disease, utilizing experimental data from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal brain chemistry by reducing the secretion of dopamine in the striatum. Despite multiple approaches to treating the symptomatology, there is currently no effective method to halt or reverse the progression of Parkinson's disease. As a result, research into the underlying mechanisms of the disease progression is crucial. In this research, a computational model incorporating the influence of dopaminergic neurons on other neurons through the re-uptake of dopamine was proposed. The model highlights the significance of dopamine uptake sites in the development of Parkinson's disease. By simulating the impact of elevated dopamine levels, the model reveals that an increase in dopamine can reverse the brain's condition. However, this benefit diminishes when dopamine reaches a certain level, indicating that this effect has a limit. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the deterioration of midbrain dopaminergic neurons can cause the abnormal accumulation of dopamine in the striatum, confirming previous findings. Additionally, the model shows that the death of more than 70% of dopaminergic neurons results in an abnormal decrease in dopamine levels in the striatum, a condition that has been observed in the advanced stages of Parkinson's disease. This model provides a theoretical basis for exploring novel treatments for Parkinson's disease through the modification of dopamine uptake sites. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of conducting further research into the relationship between dopamine levels and the progression of Parkinson's disease. This model may also be applicable to humans with Parkinson's disease, and it suggests that treatment strategies targeting dopamine uptake sites could be beneficial. This research demonstrates that there is a potential for computational models based on experimental data from marmoset monkeys to contribute to the understanding of human brain disorders. This approach could be employed to investigate other human brain disorders as well. The visual impact of map displays can be significantly improved by highlighting vector data, such as roads and boundaries. When these vector objects are rendered with a low-resolution pixel grid, a well-known distortion occurs, resulting in an aliased effect that detracts from the overall aesthetic. This distortion becomes particularly pronounced when rendering lines that are parallel to grid pixels or their orientations. To address this issue, developers have explored various techniques for improving the appearance of lines, but these methods often come with performance costs associated with increased memory usage and processing time. To balance visual effectiveness and efficiency, we examined different anti-aliasing approaches and identified a straightforward technique that effectively reduces the distortion effect with minimal performance impact. By applying this method to our sample map dataset, we achieved a noticeable visual improvement without experiencing a decline in performance. To illustrate the benefits of this approach, we included a comparison with more complex rendering methods that prioritize visual appeal but result in increased memory usage and slower rendering speeds. In line with the goal of creating fast and responsive web applications, we believe that this anti-aliasing approach represents an attractive solution for developers seeking to enhance the appearance of line joins on web maps. To facilitate exploration of this issue, we also provided a code snippet that is compatible with Google Maps and Leaflet libraries. To address the limitation of low-resolution line rendering, we explored the possibility of employing super-sampling, a technique that involves rendering lines at a higher resolution than the pixel grid. However, this approach introduced a significant performance bottleneck, outlining the need for alternative solutions. Another approach that we examined involved modifying the direction of lines to eliminate distortion effects, but this method resulted in visually unappealing lines that failed to accurately represent real-world geography. In contrast, the anti-aliasing approach that we identified met the requirement of maintaining low-resolution line rendering while achieving a high level of visual effectiveness. In response to the comment that this approach may not adequately address distortion effects on lines that are not parallel to grid orientations, we acknowledged that this issue warrants further exploration. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. Our team plans to investigate further the connection between active supermassive black holes and the outflow of gas as mergers continue and galaxies become more massive. Observations with the Seimei Telescope will allow us to study up to 20 GOALS galaxies and gather more in-depth data, with results that are expected to reveal even more intricate details. These predictions are based on models illustrating the variation of outflow as a function of merger stage and galaxy mass. Ultimately, our research with the Seimei Telescope will pave the way for even more in-depth studies with next-generation telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter-wave Array. With these powerful instruments, we will be able to examine the interaction between active supermassive black holes and the outflow of gas in galaxies at much greater distances. This in turn will enable us to better understand how galaxy mergers influence the formation of massive galaxies and the growth of active supermassive black holes throughout the history of the universe. We propose a method to entangle two atoms that were not previously correlated, using a combination of Jaynes-Cummings interactions and conditional operations. This approach allows for the generation of a wide range of entanglement metrics, including but not limited to, the formation of Bell states and Grover's algorithms, utilizing only single-qubit operations and without requiring the exchange of photons between the atoms. This proposal utilizes a three-level atom as a mediator, where two ground states in the atoms can serve as part of an entanglement system. A separate ground state in the three-level atom serves as a marker that indicates whether a particular Jaynes-Cummings interaction should occur, based on the state of a laser field. This results in either one- or two-qubit operations, depending on the state of the laser field, allowing for either the creation of an equal superposition of states or a conditional phase shift. When these conditional operations are preformed in succession, followed by the exchange of photons between the two atoms, we are able to generate a high level of entanglement between the two atoms. This effect is most prominent when the Jaynes-Cummings interaction is weak, resulting in an entanglement fraction that can reach 90%. This method also allows for the detection of entanglement, based on the outcome of these conditional operations. It should be possible to implement this proposal experimentally using current technology. This approach provides a solution to the long-standing problem of constructing a universal quantum computer, without the need for atomic interactions that result in the exchange of photons. It also offers a way to accurately place a single qubit in an arbitrary state, a crucial component for most quantum applications, and demonstrates that these operations are necessary but not sufficient for quantum computation. This proposal could serve as a foundation for further research into the interplay between single-qubit operations, conditional operations, and the entanglement of atoms. It should be possible to extend this proposal to include multiple atoms, but this would result in even more complex interactions and may not as clearly demonstrate the key points. To monitor the dynamics of quantum states in motion, we suggest using tomographic maps that incorporate both entanglement and synchronization. To illustrate the utility of these maps, we examine the evolution of a two-atom system that undergoes spontaneous emission and experiences collective effects due to its location within a cavity. A key finding is that tomographic maps can indicate critical times when significant changes in entanglement or synchronization occur, providing a precise understanding of the system's dynamics. Furthermore, we show that the information gained from these maps can be used to recover the Wigner function and a quantum correlation tomogram. We propose that tomographic maps have the potential to become a standard tool for analyzing the complex dynamics involved in quantum systems. We determine that this critical density is exactly d, meaning that at this density, the frog model is highly consistent with the behavior of the branching process. When the frog model is stable, its average degree can be compared to a closed loop on the tree, and we find that this loop has a minimum size of (d-1) / 2. Additionally, we establish that this lower bound is necessary to maintain stability. It is also possible to generalize these findings to the multi-type frog model. There, the critical density for coexistence is achieved when the sum of the squared densities for each type is equal to one. Furthermore, this relationship gives us an inequality that must be satisfied for any stable system. It is worth noting that this inequality has been previously identified as a necessary condition for the looptree model to be stable, providing further evidence of the model's relevance. 

In the case of the binary frog model, we are able to derive an exact equation that describes the average degree of any site, even when the system is highly saturated. This result comes with a straightforward proof, in contrast to the challenging proof available for the looptree model. Nonetheless, the two proofs do share some commonalities.

It is interesting to note that this number is directly related to the critical density of the frog model. Evaluating the knowledge graph embedding models' performance, however, is challenging due to the need for extensive statistical data. In contrast, a simple binary classification task can efficiently assess the models' performance. This paper proposes a novel approach to assess knowledge graph embedding models by leveraging a decision-based black-box model. Specifically, we suggest using a set of decision-based black-box models, each classified as an easy, medium, or hard sample based on their classification performance. This framework allows us to integrate the embeddings of knowledge graph samples in proportion to their classification difficulty. Our experiments demonstrate that this decision-based black-box model's guidance yields superior performance when compared to standard sampling methods. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices using their join irreducibility components, the task remains complex due to the need to identify all such components. This paper explores an approach to build the lattice of submodules of a module that is assumed to have been determined as a module decomposition into indecomposable submodules, allowing for the application of Stanley's method. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting a large number of perfectly accurate examples from human experts is very difficult due to their limited patience and willingness to make mistakes. This research tackles the more realistic challenge of imitation learning with subpar experts, where a significant portion of the provided trajectories need to be ignored because they contain errors. Let's denote the proportion of irrelevant data as $\eta$. For this problem, our main contribution is a $O(\eta^{-3}n^{3/2})$-approximate algorithm, which yields a policy within $c\eta^{3/2} \delta$ of the optimal, where $c$ depends on the number of features $n$. This achievement is significant because it implies that with only $T$ expert trajectories, where $T$ is the total number of steps, we can achieve a policy at most $O((nT)^{3/2})$ suboptimal. This result is further validated through simulations and real-world experiments. Interestingly, a previous study already established that $o(n^{3/2})$ samples would result in a $c_n$-approximate policy with an extremely small value of $c_n$. Therefore, our study lies within an important gap. The key constraint here is that we can no longer discard all irrelevant data. The algorithm we present addresses this issue by combining several techniques like careful trajectory filtering, over-approximating the reachable set, and using a novel distance metric that takes advantage of the structure of simple reachability sets. Additionally, we introduce a new variety of trajectory filter that is both computationally efficient and highly effective. This study's findings have implications for addressing noise in supervised learning and building more robust models using multiple experts with different areas of expertise. The code for our model is available at https://github.com/UM-IQC/TRAIL. The policy evaluation algorithm we developed also has utility on its own and can be found in the code repository. The theoretical results of this study are validated through experiments on both simulation and real-world data. Additionally, the study investigates the practical applications of both the TRAIL and PFE algorithms. The results of these experiments are also included in the code repository. The study also investigates the application of both the TRAIL and PFE algorithms in relation to hyperparameter selection and models with varying levels of complexity. The study finds that both the TRAIL and PFE algorithms yield more accurate models than the baseline imitation learning algorithm across all expert quality settings.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for multiple transactions to operate on the same data simultaneously. Each transaction interacts with the database through a client-side library that enforces the transaction's sequence of reads and writes. The underlying database maintains coherence by managing a cache of recently updated documents and detecting conflicts based on their history. We have analyzed the coherence mechanisms employed by MongoDB and certified that they comply with the transactional coherence criteria, establishing that conflicts are detected correctly and that the database maintains coherence for transactions that do not detect conflicts. Furthermore, we have identified scenarios in which transactions that detect conflicts may restore coherence. Our verification approach also facilitates the identification of conflicts that can be resolved, and we have validated our findings against MongoDB version 4.4.0. We have previously demonstrated the application of our approach to the transactional coherence analysis of Google's Percolate system and currently we are exploring ways to extend our approach to deal with version conflicts that can lead to data losses. The accuracy of medical image analysis models can be compromised by inherent biases present in their training datasets. This problem is particularly challenging because it's difficult to determine whether any discrepancies found between the model's predictions and actual medical results are due to flaws in the data, the model's limitations, or a combination of both. To tackle this issue, we've developed novel statistical methods to effectively identify whether any biases exist in medical image datasets and to pinpoint which specific features are likely responsible. Our approach's usefulness is demonstrated through its application to two major chest X-ray classification datasets. Notably, our techniques indicate that certain biologically plausible variations in anatomy can contribute significantly to the biases inherent in these widely used datasets. To demonstrate this, we've introduced a new unbiased dataset created through a controlled experiment and used it to train a model that performs much better when compared to models trained on biased datasets. Our research provides valuable insights that can be used to guide the development of more reliable medical image analysis models. Between 0.25 to 0.50 solar radii from the Sun's center, a solar wind stream that originates from the corona and is influenced by the Sun's rotational movement, acts as a boundary separating two distinct plasma regions. This boundary, known as the solar breeze boundary or stream interface, marks the point at which the plasma on one side of the boundary moves faster and has higher electron densities than the plasma on the other side. This boundary was previously thought to exist because of changes in the solar wind's speed and electron density, which corresponded with the time it took the solar wind to travel a certain distance from the Sun. This idea was confirmed by observing the changes in this boundary as it moved further from the Sun. The speed of the plasma on the side of the boundary moving towards the Sun had to be at least 10 kilometers per second higher than the plasma on the opposing side in order to create the energy flux that was observed. This energy flux, which was found to be in the range of 0.15 to 0.30 watts per square meter, was released back into the Sun's interior over a period of approximately three and a half days. This energy, which was converted from the mechanical energy generated by the Sun's rotational movement, played a crucial role in maintaining the stability of the Sun's core-date (the core-neutrino density) and had implications for the formation of solar flares and coronal mass ejections. These findings were based on data collected by the Parker Solar Probe's Solar Wind and Plasma Instrumentation suite during its initial stages of operation.

Thanks to speech-emotion synthesis and altered acoustic conditions in recorded data, the task of speech emotion recognition has become more complex and challenging. Pretrained models often struggle with adapting their emotions and maintaining performance in new domains, which hinders their real-world application potential. This paper proposes a novel domain adaptation technique that leverages unlabelled target domain data to adapt a pretrained speech-emotion recognition model. We employ a residual-based strategy, dividing the speech utterance into several segments with distinct emotional characteristics. We then develop a speech-emotion encoding scheme that learns to recognize emotions from a range of data. We experiment with multiple baselines and adaptators, achieving significant improvements in results and surpassing existing methods. Our results show that our proposed approach yields state-of-the-art performance on the WAVERES dataset, delivering 73.6% accuracy, a 7.6% point increase over the best previous method. We also evaluate several real-world applications involving the adaptation of models trained on US data to analyze European speech emotions. We validate our approach by conducting multiple experiments and offer insights into designing high-performance reinforcement learning systems. We release the source code of all experiments conducted with PyTorch and Keras. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  We propose that partial substitution of Bi$^{3+}$ with smaller Ti$^{4+}$ ions may counteract the structural changes, restoring magnetic order at higher temperatures.  This suggestion is to be validated through further experimentation.  This study is a first-time demonstration of using NFS in the investigation of strained materials.  It highlights the capability of NFS to explore the interplay between structure, magnetic order, and pressure in complex oxide systems.  This study offers directions for optimizing magnetic order in BFTO through chemical modification and may also be applicable to other materials investigated through NFS under high pressure conditions.  Furthermore, it showcases the potential of BFS as a sensitive probe of structural changes within materials.  This study may be expanded to explore other materials investigated through NFS under high pressure conditions, thus demonstrating the versatility of this technique.  It also highlights the necessity to consider the influence of chemical sensitivity in the selection of suitable probes for studying materials, especially those with intricate chemical compositions like BFTO. of discrete shortest paths. The accuracy of these approaches relies on the error
bound of the discrete-continuous interface, which is the maximum deviation from the
optimal solution within the continuous domain caused by a discrete starting point.
We establish a priori and a posteriori error estimates for the discrete-continuous
interface in problems involving flight trajectory optimization, providing conditions
for nearly optimal solutions when the discrete starting point is close to the boundary
of a continuously shrinking neighborhood of the optimal solution. These conditions
facilitate the implementation of backtracking in flight trajectory optimization, allowing
the recovery of optimal solutions from suboptimal discrete starting points. This
result is illustrated with examples using an adaptive mesh based on a pilot trajectory. 
We also introduce an efficient algorithm for determining suitable discrete starting
points, which identifies optimal solutions for a broader class of problems, including
those with additional constraints and objective functions. The hybrid approach we
introduce is compared to established methods for flight trajectory optimization, showing
it yields more precise solutions with a more efficient computational cost.  This error
bound is relevant to a broader class of shortest path problems and can be applied in
other contexts with similar structures.  As such, it may provide a useful reference
for researchers working in related fields.  In the context of flight trajectory
optimization, this error bound can be used to determine critical parameters, such
as the feasibility of certain discrete starting points and the level set of suboptimal
solutions, which may be of interest to researchers and practitioners.  Furthermore,
this work introduces a new paradigm for discrete-continuous optimization, which can
be used to identify optimal solutions from a given set of discrete starting points. 
This paradigm may be applicable to other areas of discrete-continuous optimization
and could provide a new framework for the development of efficient solution algorithms.

Additionally, the characteristics of the shock wave, such as temperature, density, and chemical composition, remain essentially the same as the model expands. This stability is influenced by the size of the void and the properties of the gas behind the shock wave. It has also been observed that in models without voids, shock waves can be as hot as 10 billion Kelvin, while in models with large voids, gas can be pushed out of the system. Furthermore, when considering radioactive decay as a source of energy, it could potentially balance the pressure inside the void, allowing the shock wave to resume its progression. This implies that even in models with large voids, the Earth and other planets could still be impacted by the shock waves. Research has revealed that the sounds produced have stochastic characteristics, with periodic fluctuations influenced by the rate at which the tape is peeled. A method has been developed to extract the underlying pattern by filtering out the loud noise, and the resulting signal has a regular amplitude modulation corresponding to the sound frequency. This technique has been applied to gather more data, leading to a deeper understanding of the system. A periodic signal with varying amplitude has been broken down into component parts, revealing a hidden pattern that correlates with sound intensity. A new method has been devised to model these periodic signals with different amplitude patterns, leading to the creation of a universal noise model that incorporates time-dependent signal characteristics. This model has been tested and validated using newly collected data, providing insight into the complex processes occurring during the peeling of an adhesive tape. A key parameter has been identified that influences the system's behavior, and it varies smoothly across different conditions, unlike the abrupt changes observed in sound frequency. Our experiment utilizes a unique arrangement of two superconducting loops and a thin film to study the behavior of planar Josephson junctions. We distinguish between two situations: measurements when one loop is large and the other small, and when both loops are of comparable size. The small loop exhibits minimal magnetic influence, allowing us to selectively apply a high magnetic field to induce quantized flux within it without affecting the large loop. Conversely, we can strongly influence the large loop's behavior with minimal impact on the small loop. This setup enables us to study the small loop's behavior under varying conditions of resistance and temperature, while simultaneously measuring the large loop's resistance as a function of applied magnetic field, specifically at points where the small loop's flux is an integer multiple of the fundamental quantum unit (quantization points). The resulting data reveal that the resistance of the large loop at these specific points exhibits symmetry when plotted against the resistance of the small loop, displaying distinct patterns for different temperatures. Furthermore, the resistance at these points displays a unimodal shape when considering variations in the small loop's resistance, exhibiting distinct peaks at intermediate values. The height of these peaks decreases as temperature increases, according to a characteristic power law with an exponent of -1.5 in relation to log-scaled resistance. The critical value of the small loop's resistance at the peak also varies proportionally with temperature, remaining relatively constant in terms of the small loop's resistance when changed. The underlying causes of these phenomena are attributed to the interplay between the small loop's resistance and the applied magnetic field regarding the planar Josephson junction's phase-space landscape. The resulting data provide empirical evidence for the theoretical model of symmetric cusps in the potential energy landscape, particularly in the case where the small loop's resistance is significantly higher than that of the large loop. Conversely, when the small loop's resistance is comparable to or higher than that of the large loop, the system enters a different phase, characterized by the reemergence of the zero-resistance state at quantization points, along with a different shift in the critical current's location. The results obtained from our experiments offer valuable insights into the underlying physics of planar Josephson junctions and superconducting quantum interference devices, providing a basis for further research into their unique properties.
