Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the presence of independent degree distributions that are bounded by 0 up to 1. In contrast, our research investigates LDPC ensembles when the degrees of variable nodes are not independently distributed, taking into account the influence of degree correlations. We establish a growth window for the degree distributions, which enables us to analyze the LDPC ensemble's behavior over an erasure channel and determine the maximum error correction capacity when there are degree correlations. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that in scenarios with high degree correlations, the LDPC ensemble's performance can approach the limit of an ideal random code, even with a relatively small number of code iterations. Notably, we observe that degree correlations can be beneficial in LDPC code design, particularly in situations with a large number of deletions, and a simple, practical method is proposed to generate degree distributions exhibiting desired properties. The proposed technique's effectiveness is verified through comprehensive numerical simulations in the context of binary deletion channels. Moreover, we show that there is a degree correlation threshold below which the LDPC ensemble's performance becomes identical to that of a random code, and this threshold tends to increase as the erasure probability decreases. Additionally, we find that the maximum diversity order of LDPC codes is equal to the average degree of variable nodes, and this finding is applicable not only to LDPC codes but also to other types of degree-candidate codes. Finally, we propose and analyze several general degree distribution optimization methods, and one of these methods demonstrates superior performance over a wide range of deletion probabilities. The proposed method's advantages, including its simplicity and low computational complexity, make it an attractive solution for designing and evaluating degree-candidate codes in the context of binary deletion channels. In the case of variable-node degree distributions with a maximum value of 3, a more sophisticated optimization technique can further reduce the error correction threshold by approximately 0.064 in a binary deletion channel, which corresponds to a 10% improvement over the best known results with triple-joint variable-node degree distributions. Additionally, this better performance can be achieved with much simpler code designs, such as degree distributions that only utilize single-joint variable nodes and have the same average degree as triple-joint variable nodes. In the context of binary deletion channels, we also explore another degree distribution, which we refer to as the double-joint variable-node degree distribution, and find that it can correct errors at a 0.064 lower threshold than the best single-joint variable-node degree distributions

We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to make comprehensive measurements of gas temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios. By harnessing the power of time and frequency-domain measurements, a cutting-edge technique offers unprecedented accuracy (<1%) and precision (0.42%) for detecting minor concentrations of oxygen. Initially demonstrated in a sealed environment over a pressure range (1-1.3 bar), the method effectively captures the relationship between pressure and oxygen/nitrogen ratios and maintains an error margin of pressure estimation at a manageable 0.5 bar even when the pressure reaches 1.3 bar. Notably, the method can distinguish between nitrous oxide gases with a ratio of 32.5, 33, and 33.5, enabling detection of very small quantities of nitrous oxide in nitrogens. Additionally, the method exhibits excellent performance in measuring temperature and shows no significant dependence on the presence of nitrous oxide, oxygen/nitrogen ratios, or pressure. All the measurements are achieved through a single shot, allowing for the detection of pressure and composition in gases following the expansion of an initially compressed nitrous oxide gas. With nitrous oxide emission equivalent to approximately 2200 kcal/mole, the negative enthalpy contribution is relatively small, but the high accuracy of the method makes it suitable for monitoring the composition of gases emitting a wide range of energies. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning objective in decentralized learning among interconnected nodes. We demonstrate that standard regularization methods lead to biased estimation and decrease accuracy. To overcome this issue, we apply a unique technique that minimizes the maximum expected case of an augmented loss function, subject to a constraint on the probability distribution. We then formulate an optimization problem in terms of the robust loss function and solve it using an alternative representation. We propose the DR-DSGD algorithm, based on an analysis of the optimal solution, and prove the convergence of the algorithm under specific conditions. Our experiments show that the proposed algorithm achieves superior performance compared to traditional regularization methods. Furthermore, we apply and evaluate the DR-DSGD algorithm in the context of robust cross-entropy loss for the multi-classification task and obtain results that support our theoretical findings. Recently, Forsage, a decentralized cryptocurrency investment program, has gained significant attention by promoting itself as an innovative decentralized opportunity. However, Forsage has been identified as a fraudulent pyramid scheme by multiple regulatory agencies. This paper examines the underlying structure of Forsage's code and reveals how its design facilitates deception and illegal activity. By analyzing EtherScan data and observing Forsage's operation over a two-year period, as well as data related to user transactions, the paper shows that Forsage's primary purpose is to enrich its developers and participation leaders through fraudulent means. Furthermore, it highlights the ease with which Forsage's scheme can be understood and the difficulty in implementing effective countermeasures due to its decentralized and programmable nature, indicating that similar schemes could emerge in the future. This paper also discusses the implications of Forsage's code design on the broader cryptocurrency industry and suggests potential strategies for detecting and preventing similar fraud schemes. This research is critical to raising awareness about the dangers of cryptocurrency-based fraud schemes and the importance of regulatory agencies collaborating with technology experts. By combining their knowledge, they can more effectively address the complex issues associated with the intersection of blockchain technology and financial regulations. This paper will be of value to researchers who are interested in the intersection of cryptocurrency, fraud schemes, and smart contract codes. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete, with ongoing surveys like the VVV E-band photometry revealing new potential cluster members. This study takes a detailed look at the 19 most promising candidates in the bulge region using VVV data, with no previous information about these potential clusters. By modeling luminosity profiles and analyzing radial stellar populations with VVV and OGLE-IV data, the researchers sought to verify the clusters' existence and determine their basic characteristics. However, the analysis revealed that only two of these candidates, VVV CLUS 0473 and VVV CLUS 0625, exhibited distinct luminosity profiles and population patterns, thereby confirming them as genuine globular clusters. Meanwhile, the remaining 17 candidates appeared similar to field populations and thus were found not to be clusters. This discovery implies that the bulge's globular cluster population may be more selectively revealed in reddened E-band images. Additionally, the distribution of the newly confirmed cluster and four existing globular clusters in the bulge followed a second harmonic pattern along Galactic longitudes, which may be linked to the bulge's multiple components. Furthermore, the most prominent feature in the longitude-direction diagram showed that the majority of these clusters reside on a curved structure near the bulge's plane. This study's results provide new insights into the bulge's globular cluster population and contribute to the ongoing discussion about the history and formation processes of the Milky Way. Additionally, the findings related to the distribution and population of these clusters may help to identify new cluster candidates and resolve existing debates in the field. This research took advantage of collaborative efforts between the VVV and OGLE-IV surveys and highlighted the effectiveness of using wide-area, multi-band data to map the bulge's cluster population. This study's strategies and methods can be applied to other surveys and may pave the way for further breakthroughs in the field of stellar astrophysics. The results presented in this work allow researchers to delve deeper into the behavior and life cycles of stars within these clusters, while also gaining valuable knowledge about the Milky Way's formation and evolution. This study's findings also provide a better understanding of the bulge's cluster population and may influence theoretical models of the galaxy's early history. Additionally, this research took advantage of the unique capabilities of wide-area, multi-band surveys like VVV and OGLE-IV, and the results obtained could be applied to other areas of stellar astrophysics. We examine the correspondence between microscopically derived and macroscopically described phenomena in solid-state systems that interact with light, using quantum electrodynamics in matter. A key aspect of this investigation focuses on the measure problem, which encompasses issues related to the choice of gauge and the ambiguities in charge definition. Our analysis reveals that the description of light-matter interactions depends on the selection of quantization volume and gauge, resulting in differently defined charge and spin operators. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that these variations yield equivalent physical insights, as they are connected by unitary transformations that preserve the dynamics. Consequently, we establish a basis for evaluating the effectiveness of different models and their relevance to experimental observations. Notably, we show that the proposed technique can be employed to investigate other phenomena involving light-matter interactions, as well as artificial systems with optical couplings. A tight-binding model we investigated, representing silicon doped with europium, exhibits robustness against variations in gauge and quantization, thus providing accurate description of its interaction with light, regardless of the specific details of these measures. Conversely, we found that simpler model descriptions fail to capture the complex dynamics underlying this phenomenon, highlighting the importance of maintaining the intricacies of quantum electrodynamics in model derivations. A unitary transformation is introduced to resolve the ambiguity in charge definition, resulting in a redefinition of the Wannier functions in terms of the electron's wave function and its momentum operator. This transformation expresses the measure-dependent nature of the wave function and yields a charge operator defined through the volume-independent electron density. Notably, we find that the proposed measure-invariant Hamiltonian maintains its form only when the frequency of the quantized photon field equals an integer multiple of the reciprocal lattice period, leading to a distinction between bulk and surface states and reconciling measurements made with light of different frequencies. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed technique can be applied to model artificial light-matter systems, such as superconducting circuits, by transforming Eu into a two-dimensional lattice and modifying the photon field's frequency accordingly. Text generation, a task where a model produces a realistic text based on a given context, is a complex process influenced by multiple factors, including cultural, social, and linguistic norms. Current state-of-the-art techniques, such as Generative Adversarial Networks, often struggle to create coherent and relevant text across multiple sentences. This limitation is due, in part, to the restrictive training process, which focuses on generating single-sentence outputs rather than entire text segments. To address this issue, we introduce SparseGAN, a novel sparse multigrid network that generates text in segments. By incorporating an encoder that compresses contextual input into a compact representation and a decoder that expands this representation into targeted words, SparseGAN leverages sparse attention to select relevant linguistic elements and prioritize semantic richness. Our evaluations show that SparseGAN achieves exceptional results on various text generation tasks, surpassing the performance of leading baselines and outperforming state-of-the-art GAN models while achieving a significant reduction in computational costs. Animal populations rely on external resources for vital survival functions, and understanding who uses what and where is crucial for conservation and management. Two key methods for studying animal populations are capture-recapture and resource choice studies, but they typically operate independently of each other. This work examines the effect of temperature anisotropy on the linear dynamics of geodesic acoustic modes in tokamaks. Linear gyrokinetic theory applies, and the mode frequency and growth rate are calculated in a system where the electron population is represented through a Maxwell-Gaussian distribution. Numerical simulations show that temperature anisotropy causes a significant increase in the mode frequency and a more pronounced growth rate in certain conditions, though it may become compressional and even imaginary, indicating mode instability. This effect is mitigated by finite $\beta$ effects and ion flow, though it remains significant at high electron density levels. Temperature anisotropy is found to influence ion distribution evolution critically, often leading to ion flux flattening or even peaking, and this impact persists in finite $\beta$ regimes. This work emphasizes the importance of considering temperature anisotropy for accurate interpretation of CSD measurements, particularly ion flux measurements, and may influence existing theories on ion dispersion caused by electron instabilities. Key parameters influencing this effect include the Elsmore threshold, ion flow, and $k_\perp^2$ levels, and it is recommended that temperature anisotropy be accounted for in future experiments focusing on electron flux measurement. This work also suggests linking experimental measurements of the modes' frequency and growth rate with the level of temperature anisotropy to gain deeper understanding of plasma behavior. This understanding may further be applied to develop new plasma control methods, such as actively managing temperature anisotropy to prevent mode growth. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. Blaauw's own background and vision, as well as the broader astronomical landscape at that time, are also considered. Van Rhijn's legacy as director is appraised through his achievements, shortcomings, and the legacy he left behind with the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory. This essay also examines the various forms of communication used by van Rhijn in his professional life, concluding that his written English held flaws common to many non-English speakers, did not impede his international collaboration however, and that his Dutch language skills allowed him to effectively convey complex astronomical ideas. This assessment of van Rhijn is a biographical analysis informed by primary and secondary sources. It is also a reflection on the state of astronomy in the Netherlands during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. This study serves as a foundation for further exploration into the broader cultural and scientific context within the Netherlands at that time. It is a starting point for examining how the direction of research in the Netherlands during that period, and the challenges faced, influenced the development of astronomy as a whole. We propose the theory that less expert team members ask better questions, prompting their peers to provide more accurate information. To test this idea, we created a series of simple math problems requiring two types of reasoning: logic and arithmetic. This conclusion also results in the bi-recognizability of subgroups within these groups. Additionally, we establish that fully uniform Coxeter groups are automatic, suggesting that their underlying geometry contributes significantly to the presence of recognizability. Further, we prove that the intersection of a Coxeter group and a recursive subset is also recursive, allowing us to conclude the equality of first-order definability and computability in these groups. Moreover, we establish that the decision-making capacity in lattice-ordered groups is equivalent to the capacity in their underlying Boolean algebra, and we explore the distinction between this approach and the method employed for the monoid of strictly ordered words. Moreover, we show that the group of rooted trees graded by their degree forms a bi-recognizable subgroup within the monoid of all rooted trees, offering a connection to recent findings regarding primitive groups of roots. Finally, we demonstrate that the extension of Coxeter groups to their orderings yields structures that are both bi-recognizable and first-order definable. Additionally, we prove the existence of an automaton specifying the order of words related to the Coxeter presentation, and we explore its implications on the order of elements within these groups. Furthermore, we establish that the relationship between words and their corresponding elements under these group operations is decidable, providing a foundation for further research on the computability of these structures. This theory may be applicable to a broader class of group presentations that satisfy specific conditions, and we anticipate that our results will contribute to the development of modern applied mathematics. This paper proposes a new method to estimate model selection criteria such as AIC and BIC through the use of nested sampling. Initially, a set of parameters is chosen at random and a likelihood value is determined for a given model applying those parameters. The process is then repeated with the restriction that no new parameters can be added. The method measures the average of the logarithm of the likelihood values from the subsequent samples and approximates model selection criteria accordingly. For comparison, traditional estimators rely on approximations involving the second derivative of the likelihood function, whereas our method does not require such assumptions. The method is tested on three examples: one theoretical scenario, one real-world scenario with uncertainties, and one real-world scenario with model selection. The results show our method to be a viable alternative to the traditional estimators. The method is particularly suitable for models that are difficult to compute, such as Bayesian neural networks. In random systems, the scattering matrix defines a set of eigenstates within the energy spectrum, and their superposition generates specific patterns of energy deposition. This concept of eigenstates is unique because it is rooted in the overall scattering properties of the system, rather than its internal structure. This unique perspective allows us to develop a mathematical framework that can predict deposit pattern eigenstates and their associated probabilities without needing to analyze the system's internal structure. This predictive ability is encapsulated in a fundamental equation that connects the deposit pattern eigenstates with the scattering matrix's unitary properties. This equation is expressed in terms of an expanded deposit matrix that comprises various components, each representing distinct deposit patterns that are invariant under the unitary transformation of the scattering matrix. These deposit matrix components are orthogonal to each other, and their expansion covers the entire deposit state space with unity intensity. This framework also enables the calculation of deposit cross-spectra using a simple equation that relates them to the deposit matrix components and their respective scattering matrix eigenvalues. This connection holds true for any system, regardless of whether it operates in the high-scattering regime or not. This theoretical framework is then applied to analyze scattering systems consisting of multiple scatterers by expressing the deposit matrix in terms of the properties of individual scatterers. This leads to a general deposit matrix component that is invariant under the unitary transformation of the scattering matrix and represents a fundamental pattern of energy deposition, and its associated probability is determined by the product of the probabilities of the underlying scattering matrix eigenvalues. This results in an intense deposit cross-spectra signal at frequencies that are an odd harmonic of a base frequency, and it is characterized by a narrow frequency width equal to one over the product of the frequencies and their respective scattering matrix eigenvalues. This intense signal appears only in systems with strong scattering and is not limited to systems with the same scattering properties in both space and time. This concept of deposit eigenstates and their associated probabilities provides a new perspective on scattering systems that could be exploited for enhanced energy transfer and more efficient energy-based localization and manipulation. This idea of using deposit eigenstates to achieve better understanding and control over scattering systems could be further developed for application in diverse fields such as biophotonics, thermophotonics, and metamaterials. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. Unlike traditional models, where correlations decay with distance, we investigate the impact of disorders that remain constant over several sites. Using the Toulouse-Penrose criterion and numerical transmission matrix analysis, we characterize a new type of topological state - the topological Anderson conductor - that arises when disorders are correlated in a square pattern. Additionally, we find that long-range correlations can be substituted by an equivalent short-range correlation in all directions, indicating that the TPC is robust against spatial correlation decay. Furthermore, we observe that the topological Anderson phase can be stabilized through rational tuning of a potential, and that the knowledge of disorders is not necessary to maintain this phase. Finally, we propose that sound modes in certain phononic metamaterials may exhibit the properties of a topological Anderson conductor, providing a potential pathway for their realization. Additionally, we find that localizing states in these systems can be achieved through means such as the application of a localized magnetic field, and that this has implications for the development of customized devices within the framework of active quantum management. This phenomenon can be understood by analyzing the low-energy interactions among the light Higgs bosons, heavy Higgs bosons, and the top/stop SCET fields, with contributions from top/stop wave functions and top-quark and stop scalar coefficients. A low-energy effective theory consisting of interactions among the light Higgs bosons and the top/quark is relevant for a top-quark effective heavy to light Higgs transition, occurring at a scale of a few TeV. A significant discrepancy arises when comparing the pole and on-shell definitions of the Higgs parameter, with dependence on the stop mass parameter and the mixing parameter of the top/superpartner. This difference is significant enough to be detected by a precise measurement of the on-shell Higgs decay into a pair of W bosons, with an sensitivity of the order of $10^{-4}$. Furthermore, this phenomenon exhibits sensitivity to the stop superpartner's ability to contribute to a CP-violating re-scattering effect, with implications for the search for the stop pair production in the on-shell Higgs decay into a pair of top quarks. This connection holds the potential to offer a new insight into the stop sector's properties, with the on-shell definition of the Higgs parameter serving as a probe. The magnitude of this effect is found to be independent of the heavy Higgs sector, as the on-shell definition of the Higgs parameter is blind to the heavy Higgs bosons' masses. This phenomenon introduces a new twist to the question of why the electroweak symmetry breaking occurs naturally in the MSSM. In fact, the natural electroweak symmetry breaking can be achieved even if the SCET parameters take on arbitrary complex values, as the necessary condition for this phenomenon to generate the light Higgs pole remains unchanged. This conclusion holds the potential to offer a new solution to the naturalness problem by allowing the imaginary part of the stop mass parameter to be set at a much smaller scale than the scale of the real part. Furthermore, we proactively investigate two prominent cryptocurrency scams, Panama Papers and North Korea's WannaCry, using our knowledge of currency trails. Our research produces notable results, which show that our approach outperforms existing methods and yields significantly more accurate results, especially in terms of precision. Additionally, our technique is adaptable to various cryptocurrency trail datasets with minimal adjustments required. Our research in this area continues to unfold, and we are currently exploring ways to integrate our understanding of address interaction patterns with other features, such as transaction amounts, in order to further enhance the detection of suspicious activities. We introduce a simple prediction model that considers application requirements, network characteristics, and a measure of variability known as spectral noise for predicting optimal scaling, providing a solution to the challenge of finding the balance between over-provisioning and under-provisioning. We validate this model through simulations based on real data from the Amazon EC2 cloud. We show that the incorporation of variability into the model results in a more accurate prediction of scaling than models that disregard it, reducing the risk of performance issues and downtime. We also explore the difficulty of determining the optimal scaling policy through reward-based optimization. We find that the optimal policy is difficult to identify due to the rapid change of network conditions, but we believe that this challenge can be overcome with the development of more adaptable applications. Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Notably, a key constraint in these applications is the limitation on context sharing. This paper addresses a novel problem of contextual linear bandits where context information must remain private and cannot be shared between interacting agents. This issue is further complicated due to the absence of a central controller or a shared memory. This paper proposes a novel, secure, and private learning approach for contextual linear bandits that leverages local memory and learning. This proposed approach is an extension of the classic contextual linear bandits approach but it requires only individual learning and memory sharing. This paper also proves the regret bound of this approach to be comparable to the standard linear bandits setting when context sharing is possible. This proof relies on a novel approach that utilizes the general framework of the standard linear bandits setting. This paper further provides a specific regret bound for the case when the arm selection follows a random exponential distribution. This bound is the first of its kind for this specific setting. This paper also presents an extension of this approach to a multi-armed linear bandits setting where context information remains private and arm identifiers are shared. This shared information creates an opportunity for secure learning. This opportunity is further leveraged by a novel context-dependent sampling approach. This approach results in a sublinear regret bound when the arm selection follows a random exponential distribution. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the expense of modeling individual particle collisions, it is common to simplify simulations by assuming collisions occur much faster than flow changes, which may not hold true in all situations. As a result, there is a need for more versatile simulation tools that can accurately handle shorter collision times. The new method utilizes distinct time steps for flow and particle simulations, integrating flow simulations in longer blocks of time. This method integrates the flow model over longer time steps, regardless of collision time, using a larger step size that is based on the flow model and is unaffected by particle collision time. Once flow simulations are complete, the method uses the result to advance particle positions and velocities over shorter time steps, regardless of whether collisions occur during these steps. This new method was tested against a reference simulation that used a similar flow time step but no multiple-step integration for particles, resulting in significant speedups without accurate reproduction being affected. However, it was also found that accurate simulation relies on the method's ability to detect collisions within flow time steps, which was initially missing in our current implementation. To address this issue, we introduced a new collision detection system based on particle movement relative to the flow, detecting if particles are approaching each other and are close enough to collide within the next flow time step, and adjusting the particle time step accordingly. This detection system was effective in preventing particles from skipping collisions, resulting in full reproduction of particle behavior. Notably, this new method produced similar results to simulations with no multiple-step integration method, but with significantly improved speedups. To further validate our method, we simulated the collision of two particles with different densities and time steps, with successful reproduction of known behavior. Additionally, we simulated particles with large collision time relative to the flow time step, which successfully reproduced expected behavior without flow disruption. Lastly, we simulated collisions with three particles, detecting any potential bottlenecks in our detection system, and successfully reproduced expected behavior without flow disruption, but did experience some detection system limitations. To address these limitations, we introduced an optimized detection system based on the relative speeds of approaching particles, which is more accurate and effective at detecting collisions within flow time steps, especially for particles with large collision times. This new detection system correctly handles particles with large collision times, assigning a time step based on the flow time step rather than the physical collision time, resulting in full reproduction of particle behavior. This optimized detection system significantly improves the method's performance, resulting in much faster simulation times with accurate reproduction

Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering set of reading comprehension tasks. Opposing regular comprehension tasks that focus solely on affirmatively worded passages, CONDAQA challenges models to detect and analyze the negation present in the text. A reasoner with access to diverse knowledge is necessitated to successfully interact with contemporary language, which is why we incorporate a wide range of negated statements in the dataset and make it available for public access through the Mamba platform. Established models, including pre-trained models like BART and transformer-based models like SpanBERT, have been evaluated against this standard, and our results indicate that even the most advanced models struggle to achieve substantial accuracy when confronted with the negation aspect, thus providing our team with valuable insights that can be employed to refine the CONDAQA dataset. In the process, we introduce a novel assessment named the Negation Accuracy Score, and incorporate multiple negation detection techniques into the dataset to explore possible connections between them, ultimately discovering that certain models like BART and T5 tend to rely on explicit negation markers rather than the underlying meaning of the text. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing is gradual and aims to find a ground state through modified Hamiltonian evolution, whereas quenching occurs instantly and may result in either stable or unstable outcomes due to the failure to account for system equilibration. Although quenching can lead to desirable outcome ensembles equilibrating to the desired ground states, it is often impractically difficult to achieve necessary precise symmetries in actual implementations. To overcome this challenge, we propose measuring the annealing interval at the onset of equilibrium in quenching dynamics, as this would allow for successful implementation of quantum annealing using quenching techniques. Through the application of this principle to the exact cover problem, we demonstrate its effectiveness. Furthermore, we observe that short quench delays can facilitate equilibrium outcomes with high accuracy rates, reaching as high as 90% in some instances. However, these benefits may not extend to more complex problems, as shown by an experiment involving near the end of the equilibrium interval, where the accuracy rate surprisingly drops to 1%. To better comprehend these quench dynamics, we discuss the significance of the annealing interval as it relates to the Ising Hamiltonian and the impact of quench scaling on regime transitions. We conclude that the proposed method offers a feasible pathway for overcoming the challenges associated with the implementation of quantum annealing using quenching. Additionally, it has the potential to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying this system. Moreover, we suggest that this approach may also be applicable to other problems that are computationally hard to solve in the classical world, as evidenced by the obtained results in the exact cover problem. Furthermore, we believe that this issue of rising misclassification rates towards the end of the equilibrium interval may not be unique to the exact cover problem and could be a more general phenomenon in the Ising Hamiltonian. 

In the case of the exact cover problem, we found that the accuracy rate actually decreases as we move further into the equilibrium interval, which could be a more general phenomenon in the Ising Hamiltonian.

This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while enhancing the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key improvements include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's necessary to incorporate a wide range of semantic relationships. Existing approaches that rely on representation learning tend to focus on individual aspects of semantics, such as relationships based on word similarities or syntactic patterns. In contrast, this paper advocates for an expansive relationship-based framework that leverages an extensive range of semantic relations. It introduces a novel relationship-based question answering platform that utilizes pre-trained models to automatically identify and incorporate semantic relations from a corpus. Additionally, the paper introduces a suite of 1500 questions that require a diverse set of semantic relations and evaluates how CoCo, a state-of-the-art model pre-trained on relation-inclusive datasets, performs when compared to specialized models that focus on individual semantic relations. The results show that these models perform better when they are trained with a wide range of relation-aware representations. The paper also explores the effectiveness of relation-aware pre-training and finds that it leads to consistent improvements in question answering performance across various relation types. Finally, it highlights that this approach enables question generation that is more semantically complex than other methods. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries. Additionally, these photonic devices may enable the development of handheld molecular sensors, thereby having a significant impact on various fields. We invite industry partners to collaborate with our team in further refining this technology.

The Itô-Wentzell theorem serves as a key connection between the rough path perspective on stochastic differential equations and the traditional Itô geometry. Essentially, it establishes the equivalence of solving a given SDE via the rough path perspective and the classical Itô approach. The theory has been extensively developed over the past decade in great generality. This work contributes to establishing such connections in the setting of geometric SDEs and stochastic flows, when the drift contains a component that can be expressed as a composition of a differential operator and a stochastic flow. The latter is defined in terms of the solution to a given SDE, thereby creating a circle of implications for the solvability of such equations. The Itô-Wentzell theorem is a fundamental result that enables us to determine the pathwise uniqueness of solutions to SDEs, which in turn allows us to establish the existence of solutions in a geometric setting. The existence, in turn, implies the uniqueness of solutions in the same setting, where the driving noise is governed by a geometric SDE. This duality of implications holds a significant interest. The theory is highly general, covering a vast array of noise processes, including geometric beta-stable, geometric Brownian motion, and even noise processes with non-explosion bounds. The results are established for a vast class of functions, including monotone operators and quasilinear operators with multiple variables. The theory is also extended to cover the case of differential operators with distributional solutions, which includes fractional operators such as the Laplace operator, subject to certain conditions. The results are proven for a vast array of rough paths, including rough paths with exponential moments of any order, which provide a vast generalisation of the traditional Itô-Wentzell theorem. In the current era of artificial intelligence, there is a growing need to combine data from diverse devices and platforms for training global models. However, gathering extensive amounts of data for training remains a challenge due to existing methods requiring centralized access and standardized data formats. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel approach to federated learning that leverages random walks to learn from disparate datasets. Our method enables each device to contribute to the global model through a random walk process, eliminating the need for standardized data and enabling the combination of large amounts of heterogeneous data. We evaluate our approach against conventional federated learning and observe significant improvements in accuracy on various datasets and networks, with gains of up to 200% in certain cases. Notably, our approach allows for the combination of non-IID data without the need for complex optimizations, resulting in highly efficient training times. We open-source our framework at https://github.com/UMI-COMET/Stroll. Additionally, we introduce the Cometes Challenge, a prominent research competition focused on heterogeneous device collaboration, with the aim of advancing the field through innovative solutions. Stroll has achieved top rankings in this challenge, surpassing state-of-the-art federated learning baselines by substantial margins of up to 213%. To facilitate further breakthroughs, we release the challenge's detailed statistics and key findings at https://www/cometes-challenge.org/. We introduce an optimized variant of Stroll, titled Stroll2, that further minimizes communication costs and achieves even greater accuracy gains of up to 300%. Stroll2 has also secured top ranks in the Cometes Challenge, exceeding state-of-the-art federated learning baselines by significant amounts of up to 267% in certain cases. We investigate the theoretical aspects of Stroll and derive a novel bound for random walk-based federated learning under certain conditions, providing insights that can be applied to various random walk parameters. We explore various optimization techniques, including proximal optimization and convergent guarantees, that can be integrated with Stroll to further improve its performance. We validate the efficacy of Stroll on multiple open-source datasets and research frameworks, including SplitBrain, NCMINIST, and MXNet, and observe accurate results with low error rates. We examine the computational resources required by Stroll and compare them with those of conventional federated learning, revealing that Stroll requires substantially more resources due to complex random walk calculations, although it delivers significantly better performance. Three-dimensional wave turbulence within a finite domain is examined in a numerical study that uses high-resolution direct numerical simulations. The analysis focuses on the evolution of the one-dimensional energy spectrum in the direction perpendicular to wave propagation, and it confirms that three-dimensional isotropic conditions are met when the wave number is high. However, when the wave number is low, the energy spectrum deviates from a power law, resulting in a maximum energy density that increases with time in a fixed proportion to the mean energy density across that particular range. This distortion decreases as the ratio of the wave number to the total energy in the spectrum decreases. Once the spectrum reaches the inertial range in three-dimensional isotropic conditions, where the energy density is proportional to the power of three over nine, further changes in the spectrum are governed by the same proportion as before, until the spectrum is fully released in a short period of time due to the simulation coming close to a stationary state. The time it takes for this release to occur is similar to that of a three-dimensional decaying isotropic simulation, where the same proportion that the energy density follows is diagnostic of the dissipation rate. The research finds that the distortion in the two-dimensional energy spectrum is a universal feature of simulations conducted over a broad range of parameters, and it is confirmed that the spectrum follows the same proportion as before once three-dimensional isotropic conditions are met, providing evidence for the existence of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum in the case where the phase space is not fully released. The opportunity is also taken to verify the accuracy of the simulations against established theories and to identify the source of an apparent discrepancy in the data of Castano-Kova et al. ("Strong local intense wave structure dynamics and statistics in three-dimensional wave turbulence", 2019). The results show that the discrepancy arises from the fact that the phase space is not fully released after a relatively short time compared to the lifetime of the simulations, and therefore, the spectrum does not continue to follow the predicted power law in this regime. Additionally, the research confirms that the simulations are consistent with the expected scaling when the phase space is fully released, or when the proportion that the energy density follows is diagnostic of the dissipation rate, and it confirms that the simulations conserve the properties of zero mean and unit variance. This paper examines how court-ordered mental health treatment for the convicted affects their future criminal activity and employment prospects.  It uses data from over 700,000 individuals in California who were required to undergo mental health treatment as part of their probation and compares them to a similar group of the convicted who did not receive treatment.  It finds that individuals required to undergo mental health treatment have a lower likelihood of being re-arrested and being employed in the future by about 1-2%.  However, it also finds that it has no impact on future violent crime and only has a small positive effect on employment among young males with lower levels of education.  It concludes that making mental health treatment optional rather than mandatory could lead to 3-6% more of the convicted being re-arrested.  It also finds that there are significant differences in the effect of mental health treatment on future crime and employment depending on the individual's level of education and age.  It suggests that one possible reason for the difference in future crime and employment is that optional mental health treatment may provide convicted individuals with an incentive to focus on rehabilitation.  It also suggests that courts and corrections departments may want to consider making mental health treatment optional rather than mandatory for certain groups of the convicted in order to increase its effectiveness.  It uses a quasi-experimental research design to answer these questions.  It accounts for many potential differences between individuals who were required to undergo mental health treatment and those who were not by including controls for their characteristics, the characteristics of the crimes they committed, and the mental health courts and corrections departments served.  It also accounts for many potential differences arising from the fact that required mental health treatment may attract more serious or more difficult-to-treat cases by including controls for the length and type of sentence imposed, the type of crime committed, and the presence of additional charges.  It accounts for many potential differences arising from the fact that individuals who were required to undergo mental health treatment may have different expectations about their future criminal activity and employment prospects by including controls for their self-reported expectations about their future crime and employment. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its simplicity, which prevents the risk of model distortion associated with other techniques. Our experiment involves comparing this approach to other methods, including entropy and cross-entropy, using a publicly available MRI brain segmentation dataset provided by the MICCAI 2018 Challenge. The results show that this simple regularization technique outperforms existing methods, achieving a dice similarity coefficient of 0.8746. This method's effectiveness is further validated through further experiments conducted on two additional datasets. Our research indicates that this technique is a reliable solution for addressing the limited annotations issue in medical image segmentation. The code for this study has been made available online at the specified URL. Furthermore, the model's weights have been uploaded to the established platform, from which they can be downloaded for use on additional brain segmentation datasets. This model's performance places it among the top-performing submissions from the 2018 challenge. It should be noted that this model was trained and tested prior to the introduction of advanced contrast enhanced datasets in 2019. Therefore, models like ours, which rely heavily on tissue density information, may not achieve the same level of performance on more recent challenge datasets. Nonetheless, this technique remains a viable method for addressing the lack of detailed pixel-level annotations in medical image segmentation tasks. The relatively simple nature of this approach makes it an attractive solution for other image segmentation applications involving limited annotations. Additionally, this technique's efficacy is further validated by our observation that entropy-based methods, although not directly applicable to this problem, do indicate the importance of data normalization when achieving optimal results. This, in turn, leads to a further insight that our proposed technique can be viewed as a form of normalized multi-task learning strategy. This perspective provides a theoretical justification for this method's effectiveness. This understanding can be extended to other similar problems involving the segmentation of non-tracable objects from partial annotations. For the Large Hadron Collider in CERN, the ATLAS experiment's jet calorimeter trigger system must quickly identify high-energy jets resulting from complex particle collisions. To achieve this, the system utilizes a multilevel architecture, integrating full-detector data within 40 microseconds. Our research focuses on the second-level circuitry, where a subset of high-energy jets are processed to identify heavy particles characteristic of certain collisions. We have designed an improved version of the 2LJ-ULTRA board, which uses an advanced Xilinx Kintex UltraScale+ chip to determine the properties of particles such as top quarks, Higgs bosons, and vector bosons. By leveraging the capabilities of this chip, the system can deliver 10 megajoules of power within 40 nanoseconds while handling 30 megabits of data per second. To maintain system reliability, the design includes redundant components, as well as a cooling system and a management circuit using a Texas Instruments TMDSCN073Q driver. We have successfully tested the fully assembled board and are now integrating it into the jet calorimeter trigger system with expected deployment in 2019.

The generalized maximum likelihood estimation method is a powerful tool for updating the average parameter of a mixture when the mixture components are unknown. Knowledge tracing, a field focused on modeling student knowledge, has emerged over the past decade, leveraging educational data to understand student learning patterns. Various knowledge tracing techniques have been developed to measure the connection between a student's existing knowledge and new skills acquired through education. In recent years, deep learning methods have gained significant attention in this domain, thanks to advancements in computer hardware and the development of sophisticated neural network architectures. To facilitate and accelerate research in this area, we have created pyKT, an open-source Python library designed to streamline the process of building, evaluating, and comparing deep learning-based knowledge tracing models. This paper outlines the features of pyKT and its impact on the knowledge tracing community. Furthermore, we introduce a novel metric called the pyKT Score, which evaluates the effectiveness of deep learning-based knowledge tracing models and facilitates fair competition among researchers. We have employed pyKT to re-examine the submissions made to the 2020 Knowledge Tracing Competition, and the re-implemented codes have been made available on GitHub through continuous integration. Lastly, we outline potential directions for future research enabled by pyKT, including its application to cross-domain knowledge tracing, partial action data, and multistep knowledge tracing. We have made pyKT an open-source repository, and it has been incorporated into the Knowledge Tracing Competition 2022, featuring a new challenge related to multistep knowledge tracing. Additionally, we have introduced a knowledge tracing leaderboard, available at https://knowledge-tracing.org/leadership, and we have established the Knowledge Tracing Organization to guide the development of strong models through rigorous evaluation methods. We have also introduced an official GitHub repository for the Knowledge Tracing Competition, located at https://github.com/ knowledge-tracing-competition, and we have created a Discourse forum for the Knowledge Tracing Community at https://discourse.knowledge-tracing.org/. We have established an association with the Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Education (CAI) and have submitted an abstract for our work, which will be presented at the conference. We have obtained funding from the National Science Foundation through the grant number 2044520, and we have obtained institutional review board (IRB) approval for our research, obtaining a certificate of exemption for studies involving educational data, which can be found at https://www.pitt.edu/~committees/irb/reports/2022-2023/IRB2022-03553.pdf. We have registered pyKT with the Penn State University's Technology Transfer Office and have obtained a software license from the university.

Unlike existing SMT formats such as SMT-LIB, Alethe is designed from the ground up with a focus on the underlying constraints and assumptions necessary for SMT solving, in contrast to the legacy-based approach of SMT-LIB. As a result, Alethe produces more compact and readable input files, eliminating the need for the SMT-LIB front-end translator typically required for SMT solvers. Our format is inherently adaptable to various SMT solvers and SMT-based verification tools, offering enhanced support for popular solvers like Z3, CVC4, and VeriT. To demonstrate the utility of Alethe, we showcase its effectiveness with a range of benchmarks and SMT problems, highlighting its benefits in terms of problem understanding, solvers' insights, and new research possibilities. As an open-format proposal, Alethe is being made available for feedback and input from the SMT community. As such, we have released the format under a permissive license to facilitate exploration and expansion of its concepts by researchers and practitioners. Graph mining applications rely heavily on node embeddings that preserve structure and proximity. To test the validity of novel node embedding techniques, a limited range of benchmark datasets is typically used. In this study, a new diverse social network dataset, Twitch Players, has been created to provide a range of target attributes. The evaluation of the social network and the results of the node classification experiments confirm that Twitch Players can effectively assess the performance of novel node embedding algorithms. The dataset and the source code are available for public use. To overcome the limitations of existing target attributes in social network datasets, a new approach has been introduced that utilizes structural role-based node labeling. This approach has been incorporated into the Twitch Players dataset to prevent the overfitting of node embedding algorithms to target attributes that are merely proximal. Instead of relying on random initializations, this approach uses a form of node labeling that is resistant to variations in initial conditions and produces more consistent results. The results of the node classification experiments confirm that target attributes that are resistant to variations in initial conditions produce more consistent results and are less prone to overfitting. The influence of the labeling strategy on the performance of the node classification algorithm has been investigated and found to be dependent on the specific algorithm used. The results show that the performance of the node classification algorithm is better when the target attributes are more homogeneous. The influence of the labeling strategy is more pronounced in smaller graphs. The results of the node classification experiments can be reproced with a range of novel node embedding algorithms that preserve structure and proximity. The target attributes that are resistant to variations in initial conditions are achieved using a form of node labeling that is based on the algorithmic fairness framework and reduces the disparity in labels across the network. This form of node labeling has several advantages over traditional methods, such as avoiding the construction of a proximity graph, avoiding the selection of a single nearest neighbor, and avoiding the use of a pre-defined threshold to determine the proximity of nodes. Additionally, this form of node labeling allows for the incorporation of external attributes that can influence the labels of the nodes. A major limitation of series elastic actuators is their lack of precise force control, mainly due to uncertain transmission dynamics affecting their motor control system. This study presents a novel approach to accurately regulate the force at the elastic element, despite these uncertainties. This method, known as the transmission force observer, uses state feedback fusion to combine measurements from the motor and elastic elements to estimate the transmission dynamics' impact on force. This observation enables the inclusion of a compensation term in the control system, effectively mitigating the adverse effects of transmission dynamics on force control. This approach is theoretically robust to various types of model discrepancies and transmission disturbances. Experimental results on an actual SEA platform demonstrate the efficacy of this method, showing it can achieve accurate force control even in the presence of significant transmission dynamics. This research provides a solution to one of the key challenges associated with series elastic actuators. It enables their widespread use in applications requiring precise force control, such as surgery, heavy-industry robotics, and vehicles, by providing a reliable and accurate force control system. This study also presents a design framework for optimal transmission dynamics in future SEAs, where robust force control is a top priority. This framework involves trading off energy storage capacity and the actuator's power efficiency against its power transmission efficiency. It is particularly relevant to power-efficient energy-based control methods, such as those employed in rubber-series elastic actuators and electroactive polymer actuators. This study facilitates the design of high-performance, force-regulating SEAs through their transmission dynamics. We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate scalar fields with varying charges and masses. These scalar fields are represented by either real values (x, y, z) or complex quaternion algebras, corresponding to different symmetries (O(Nf), U(Nf) etc.). The presence of a 't Hooft-like coupling allows for exact calculations using the exact lattice partition function and multiple duality relations. This leads to multiple possible competition patterns of the symmetry-breaking Higgs phases and a nearby deconfinement phase within the phase diagram. The Higgs phases exhibit Nf scalar condensation and colorless meson operators that possess a high order and are relevant for the confinement mechanism. The impact of these theories might be observable in the universe, particularly in the cosmological contexts of the early universe or in the supercooling process of nucleon formation. Additionally, these theories hold the key to better understanding the physics of quark condensation and the confinement mechanism within QCD. The calculations involve complicated polynomial equations that describe the phase diagrams, and this knowledge can be gained through the publically available Mathematica notebook provided in the appendix. The provided equations bring the essential features of the SU(Nc) gauge theories with multi-parameter scalar fields clearly into focus, featuring an highly intricate interplay of competition patterns that are influenced by the charge and mass of the scalar field. This intricate interplay results in multiple Higgs phases that are distinguished by various symmetry groups and is a unique phenomenon that is only observable in 3D lattice theories. It is crucial to note that the presence of a mass matrix that is positively defined is a necessary condition for the emergence of the Higgs phase in these SU(Nc) gauge theories. This condition ensures that the potential has a local minimum at the origin, allowing for the formation of a condensate. A negatively defined mass matrix, on the other hand, would result in an imaginary self-energy, indicating that the scalar field acquires a purely imaginary mass and becomes a Goldstone boson that is massless. A further analysis of these theories, namely when the charge matrix has a positive eigenvalue and the mass matrix has a negative eigenvalue, reveals that the resulting theory is a coexistence phase of two Higgs phases that are distinguished by different symmetry groups. A simple generalization allows us to extend this concept to charge and mass matrices with multiple negative eigenvalues, giving rise to a multi-Higgs phase that comprises multiple distinct Higgs phases

This paper introduces a novel artificial neural network model called Arranging Networks (ANs), which comprises layers that systematically rearrange input data. Unlike conventional neural networks that ANs relies on spatial and temporal rearrangements to process information. Our anointed model includes three distinct patterns: temporal stacking, spatial nesting, and nested nesting. Uniquely, nested nesting allows for the incorporation of external knowledge through matching prerequisites. ANs have been applied to solve the mutual exclusion problem and facilitate the recognition of patterns, as demonstrated mathematically. Additionally, experiments have shown that ANs can solve diverse problems efficiently, outperforming traditional neural networks in certain instances. Furthermore, the authors propose an unsupervised training algorithm for ANs based on the principle of maximum likelihood estimation. This method is akin to the backpropagation technique used to train conventional neural networks. However, unlike backpropagation which computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to network weights, the proposed method estimates the probability of accurate arrangement as a function of spatial and temporal constraints. This probability is then utilized to estimate the likelihood of accurate arrangement under given constraints, and this estimation process mirrors the computation of gradient in backpropagation. A case study is also presented where the proposed network successfully recognizes spatial patterns in arranging sequences and demonstrates that this pattern recognition capability is similar to that of recurrent neural networks. A key advantage of ANs is that they require substantially fewer network layers than traditional neural networks to achieve comparable performance. For instance, an AN with just three layers can perform tasks that require over a hundred layers in a traditional neural network. A major shortcoming of ANs, however, is that they are highly specific to pre-defined patterns and thus have difficulty in generalizing to new situations. This problem is further exacerbated when the patterns to be recognized are similar but occur in different time frames or sequences. As a result, ANs often struggle to recognize patterns that repeat over extended periods of time or patterns that occur in different temporal or spatial domains. This difficulty in pattern recognition is due to the unique way in which information is processed in ANs. Unlike conventional neural networks that process all past information equally, ANs only consider the information contained in the current time frame or spatial domain. This limitation results in ANs overlooking critical information that occurs outside of their defined window, and therefore they fail to recognize patterns that repeat over extended periods of time or patterns that occur in different temporal or spatial domains. Nonetheless, ANs offer a novel perspective on sequence processing that highlights the significance of spatial and temporal arrangements in machine learning

We propose a new anisotropic stellar object model in General Relativity, which is composed of two fluids sharing a common four-dimensional spacetime. The model's energy conditions are examined under the assumption that one fluid's energy density always exceeds the other's, resulting in an anisotropic stress tensor. Using an expansion in Taylor series for the potential of the more dense fluid, we derive a series of equations that describe the behavior of static, spherically symmetric objects in both non-relativistic and relativistic scenarios. Through numerical solutions, we demonstrate how the model's properties relate to the two fluids' respective energies in both cases. Consequently, we find that in the non-relativistic regime, objects composed of two fluids exhibit similar properties to those with a single fluid, yielding the same equation of state. By contrast, in the relativistic regime, objects with a same-energy dual-fluid configuration experience a degree of gravitational compression that is half as much as that of objects with a same-total energy where the energy is entirely held by one fluid. Moreover, the model predicts the existence of dual-fluid objects with same-total energy but uneven distributions of energy density, at a range of compressibility values in between the half and no compression extremes. These objects would predominantly comprise a highly compressible fluid with a small amount of incompressible fluid, where the compressible fluid's pressure remains directly correlated with its energy density. This model of dual-fluid objects broadens our understanding of relativistic objects and may have implications for the study of neutron stars. It suggests that if a star composed of two fluids, where one holds a small proportion of the total energy and the other holds the remainder, has a same-total energy but uneven energy density distribution, it would exhibit a range of compressibility values, where the more dense fluid is highly compressible and the less dense fluid is incompressible, resulting in the pressure of the more dense fluid being directly correlated with its energy density. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO$_3$ using synchrotron radiation and resistivity measurements under high external magnetic fields. Findings show that this material exhibits a unique 2D centered-honeycomb crystal structure, displaying a transition from an isotropic to an anisotropic resistivity at temperatures around 200 K under high magnetic fields. Additionally, the resistance becomes linear with increasing magnetic field strength across the Néel antiferromagnetic order of Gd ions. A simple model indicates that the observed anisotropy and linear resistivity change arise due to the interference of a long-range exchange field on the motion of In ions. This interpretation is validated by the results of Monte Carlo simulations, which demonstrate a similar resistance behavior in GdInO$_3$. Furthermore, the resistance change exhibits a strange magnetic-field dependence, displaying a sudden shift at fields above 20 T, which is attributed to the modification of the antiferromagnetic order of Gd ions. This modified order causes a change in the exchange field's direction, leading to a shift in the energy of the In ions. This understanding provides a basis for predicting similar resistivity changes in other hexagonal honeycomb materials with antiferromagnetic ions. Conversely, the extraordinary magnetic characteristics of GdInO$_3$ suggest that this material may not be an ideal representation of a perfect, unpinned two-dimensional antiferromagnetic state. Instead, it exhibits a unique, closely balanced competition between isotropic and anisotropic spin arrangements, making it an intriguing candidate for further research in the physics of frustrated systems.

This problem requires a balance between distinguishing individuals who look similar and grouping individuals who have the same appearance but have been captured on different occasions. It becomes even more complex when dealing with large datasets, as it's not only identifying individuals in a single frame but also in a video sequence with thousands of frames. We propose a novel, unsupervised re-identification approach that utilizes contrastive learning to tackle this problem, breaking it down into two main components: same-person vs. different-person comparison and camera matching. For same-person vs. different-person comparison, we employ a contrastive learning technique with a focus on reducing similarity differences and expanding to process video sequences. It produces a same-person code that not only captures an individual's unique features but also their temporal characteristics. By combining these code types and applying non-linear interpolation, we can accurately predict an individual's code for video segments and achieve state-of-the-art performance on large-scale datasets, including the FIERY and OULVIS datasets. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Simulation results show this scheme offers a significant gain of up to 8 dB in pilot reuse cases and 5 dB in non-reusable pilots scenarios for a 1% mismatch likelihood, and a smaller but still notable improvement in larger pilot sequences. We introduce a novel approach known as model-space quantum simulations within the framework of quantum fictitious time evolution, allowing us to efficiently simulate multiple states simultaneously. This method leverages an implicit expansion of the time-dependent wave function using a model space that is similar to the umbrella sampling method in classical simulations, enabling us to achieve significant gains in efficiency, up to the square of the number of states. The reason for this shape is not exclusively atmospheric pressure but is instead likely a result of the interaction between the developing polar vortex and a persistent temperature gradient in the planet's northern hemisphere. Our high-bias photoemission electron microscopy and surface-sensitive spectroscopies reveal that vacuum surface exposure significantly alters the film's properties, activating a large number of adsorbate atoms that act as electron traps. This finding is corroborated by large-scale arrangements of vacuum-induced pits, which serve as indicators of the electron's mobility. As a result, the mid-bias electron mobility is reduced by two orders of magnitude, and the activation energy is increased by 0.3 eV, explaining the insulating behavior typically observed in as-prepared V$_2$O$_3$ films. Additionally, we show that annealing in vacuum eliminates the adsorbate layer, restoring the trap-free condition and the films' initial metallic characteristics. Furthermore, our findings indicate that oxygen annealing, often employed to control the transition, instead introduces an intermixed oxygen-vanadate layer that acts as a variable trap depth, allowing for continuous adjustment of the activation energy. These breakthroughs hold significant implications for research involving surface-sensitive properties in transition metal oxides. Additionally, they highlight the importance of rigorously controlling the vacuum surface modification of films and substrates in order to accurately interpret results, especially when studying phase transition phenomena. This concept may also be applicable to other materials with exposed active surfaces. We find a specific scaling in time that leads to the precise measurement of Bose-Einstein condensation fraction in quasi-confinite systems. We also demonstrate that a critical point exists in the quantum double dark-soliton state, where the condensate fraction remains constant despite changes in magnitude due to scattering. This phenomenon is illustrated through correlation measurements. We confirm our findings with Monte Carlo simulations. We analyze the time-evolved state using an initial state matrix product simulation, and our results for condensate fraction and correlation with an imaginary time evolution are comparable to our Monte Carlo simulations. We observe that the quantum double dark-soliton state behaves like a persistent mode of operation for the boson gas, exhibiting universal characteristics that are unaffected by initial conditions. This implies that this state could be an suitable model for studying many-body physics in scattering environments. This study was conducted using an initial state matrix product simulation, a quantum Monte Carlo simulation, and a linear regression analysis.
